The Author

About the Author

Steve Wolf is an expert witness whose work includes maritime, drowning, and SCUBA injury cases. He is a NAUI-certified SCUBA instructor, a rescue diver, and an experienced Emergency Medical Technician. He holds a B.A. from Columbia University and has written eleven patents. His experience as a private investigator includes developing evidence in the field.

Wolf evaluates physical evidence, records, witness accounts, and applicable standards. Each opinion requires a connection between the evidence reviewed and the specific question addressed.

Wolf has served as a maritime safety officer, rescue diver, and safety diver on movie sets. He served on the Shelby County Sheriff’s Office Dive Team and holds seventeen FEMA certifications relevant to water rescue, incident command, and hazard analysis. His investigations address equipment, site conditions, operations, and rescue procedures within the scope of his qualifications.

Wolf has appeared on CNN, Fox News, MSNBC, and NewsNation to explain technical subjects. He can be reached at Steve@SteveWolfExpertWitness.com, (512) 653-9653, or SteveWolfExpertWitness.com.

Foreword

How to Use This Book

An aquatic-injury investigation begins with the reported event, the available evidence, and the questions that remain unresolved. Identify the people, equipment, operating conditions, and legal relationships before selecting a causal theory.

Physical conditions and records can change after an incident. Maintenance can alter equipment, currents can change, and recording systems can overwrite data. Early preservation and qualified examination help establish what remains available and what cannot reliably be reconstructed.

Chapters 2 and 14 address diving and causation. Chapters 3 through 7 address pool operations, standards, visibility, and surveillance. Chapters 8 and 9 address electrical injury and maritime law. Chapters 10 through 12 address boating, personal watercraft, and decided cases. Chapter 13 separates public reporting about Ian Gumbs from unresolved questions. The discovery and investigation chapters provide checklists to adapt to the evidence and jurisdiction.

For each cited standard, establish its scope, edition, adoption, and application to the activity. Distinguish a legal requirement from a contractual undertaking, a training instruction, and a recommended practice. Compare the relevant provision with the evidence rather than assuming a departure or compliance.

An expert should evaluate evidence that supports and challenges each proposed explanation. Equipment condition, human actions, environmental conditions, and medical factors may interact. The report should explain the weight assigned to each and identify unresolved uncertainty.

Introduction

Why Water Cases Are Different

Aquatic injuries can require investigation of changing water conditions, equipment, human actions, and medical events. The available evidence may support several interacting mechanisms rather than a single cause.

A site inspection records conditions at the time of inspection. Establish how those conditions differ from the incident through photographs, maintenance records, environmental data, and witness accounts. Preserve physical items and original electronic records before avoidable changes occur.

Potential authorities include health and construction codes, federal statutes, navigation rules, training standards, and operator policies. Their application depends on the jurisdiction, activity, claimant’s status, and incident date. A document’s relevance does not establish that every provision governs the case.

Physical analysis can estimate forces, pressure changes, visibility, and movement when the inputs support those estimates. Medical analysis addresses injury, incapacitation, treatment, and prognosis. Neither supplies a complete liability analysis without the evidence of conduct, the governing duties, and the applicable causation standard.

Chapter 1

The Anatomy of Aquatic Injury Cases

Aquatic injuries can involve immersion, vessel contact, equipment malfunction, exposure, or falls aboard a vessel or near the water. Identify the alleged injury mechanism and the duties of each participant without assuming that one category excludes another.

The families of aquatic injury cases

Classifying the incident helps identify preservation needs and potential areas of expertise. A single event may involve product design, operating procedures, premises conditions, and medical questions.

Open-Water Drowning

Open-water investigations may involve current, depth changes, visibility, temperature, weather, access, warnings, and rescue resources. Identify who controlled the activity or location and what duties the governing law imposed. Assess the participant’s knowledge and conduct alongside the operator’s actions; the invitation to enter the water alone does not establish liability.

Pool and Spa Drowning

Pool and spa investigations may involve barriers, depth markings, drains, water quality, lighting, surveillance, and emergency response. Identify the applicable requirements and reconstruct the incident before deciding which conditions contributed to the injury.

SCUBA Fatalities

SCUBA investigations may involve equipment condition, breathing gas, dive planning, supervision, diver actions, and medical events. Preserve the equipment, available computer data, and medical evidence. Evaluate potential interactions rather than assuming an equipment defect, an operator breach, or diver fault. See Chapter 2.

Maritime and Vessel Accidents

An injury aboard or near a vessel may raise maritime jurisdiction and choice-of-law questions. Evaluate the location, activity, claimant’s status, and relationship to the vessel. Those findings affect available claims and remedies but do not resolve factual causation. See Chapter 9.

Watercraft and personal-watercraft injuries

Separate the event involving the vessel from the injury to each occupant. Preserve evidence of collisions, flooding, overturning, falls overboard, propulsion contact and escape. Retain the experts needed to evaluate the actual vessel and medical mechanism. See Chapters 10 through 13 for watercraft investigation, decided cases and a neutral account of a current matter.

Electric-Shock Drowning

Consider electrical exposure when an incident occurs near energized equipment or witnesses report shocks or loss of movement. An electrical investigation and medical review are needed to evaluate that possibility. A drowning diagnosis or absence of burns alone does not resolve whether electrical exposure contributed. See Chapter 8.

Cruise-Ship Incidents

Cruise claims may involve passenger-ticket terms governing notice, filing deadlines, forum, and choice of law. Obtain the actual contract and check its enforceability, applicable statutory protections, and any exceptions. Calendar potential deadlines while the jurisdictional analysis proceeds.

Resort and Hotel Aquatic Injuries

Identify the entities that owned, operated, managed, maintained, and controlled a resort’s aquatic facilities. Examine contracts, actual practices, access, warnings, and staffing. Corporate affiliation alone does not establish operational control or responsibility.

Plaintiff and Defense Postures

The plaintiff must prove the elements of the claim under the applicable burden of proof. The defense may challenge that proof and may bear separate burdens on affirmative defenses. Do not substitute the criminal-law phrase “reasonable doubt” for the civil standard.

Assess preservation needs promptly: equipment, logs, inspection records, maintenance history, and original recordings. Delay may restrict reconstruction, but its effect depends on what evidence survives and what other reliable sources are available.

Both sides should investigate before avoidable changes to the scene or equipment. Evaluate comparative fault, assumption of risk, and causal connection under the governing law. Parental inattention and an operator’s failure can coexist; neither should be assumed to exclude the other.

Identifying the expertise needed

An aquatic incident may occur outside a witness’s view or involve a mechanism unfamiliar to a lay observer. Video, testimony, equipment, and medical records can each supply part of the sequence. Identify their limitations rather than dismissing an entire category of evidence.

Retain specialists for questions that require their knowledge, training, or experience. The need for expert testimony and its admissibility depend on the issues and governing rules. Early consultation can guide preservation and testing without committing the expert to a conclusion.

Early expert involvement

Identify time-sensitive evidence and the expertise needed to examine it. Record what has changed and evaluate how those changes limit, rather than necessarily defeat, the investigation.

Fluid Dynamics and Hydrostatics in Causation Analysis

Hydrostatics and fluid dynamics can help evaluate pressure, buoyancy, flow, and forces. Use a calculation only when the available inputs, assumptions, and uncertainty support the question being addressed.

Hydrostatics: The Physics of Water at Rest

Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth at roughly one atmosphere for every 33 feet of seawater. Pressure changes are relevant to breathing-gas use, gas expansion, and decompression. Buoyancy depends on displaced water and total weight, including equipment; a diver’s motion also depends on swimming effort, gas volume, and other conditions.

Fluid Dynamics: The Physics of Water in Motion

Moving-water analysis may address drag, drain suction, recirculating flow, and thermal conditions. For a simplified drag model, force varies with the square of relative velocity when density, projected area, and drag coefficient remain constant. A real swimmer’s posture and motion can change those inputs. State the model’s assumptions before applying its result to a person.

A numerical result does not establish reliability by itself. Document the measurements, model, uncertainty, and alternative explanations. Explain which conclusions the calculation supports and which require additional evidence.

The Litigation Timeline: A Preview

Preservation, investigation, pleading, discovery, expert disclosure, and trial preparation overlap. Jurisdiction and deadlines may require action before technical analysis is complete. Update the investigative plan as new evidence changes the questions.

Repairs, servicing, or rewiring may alter evidence. Compare preincident records, removed parts, witness accounts, and any available exemplars before deciding what can still be tested. Distinguish a lost opportunity for a particular test from a conclusion that the entire case cannot be reconstructed.

Common Threads Across All Case Types

Across these cases, examine physical conditions, human actions, medical findings, and applicable duties. Some incidents have extensive records; others do not. Do not transfer a supervision rule, technical model, or inference from one activity to another without examining its fit.

Organize the analysis by proposition: the evidence supporting it, contradictory evidence, assumptions, and remaining uncertainty. Revise the conclusion when the balance of evidence changes.

Chapter 2

SCUBA Fatality Litigation

A SCUBA fatality can involve several interacting events before and after the diver loses the ability to self-rescue. Equipment, breathing gas, the dive profile, environmental conditions, supervision, and medical history require separate examination and an integrated reconstruction.

Equipment condition, diver actions, and other contributors

Equipment failure and diver actions are not mutually exclusive explanations. Preserve the regulator, buoyancy compensator, cylinder, weights, computer, gauges, mask, and fins as recovered. Compare their condition with the dive records, witness accounts, and medical findings.

Testing may reveal a malfunction or contamination, but an intermittent failure may not recur during inspection. A computer may record depth without cylinder pressure, breathing rate, or the diver’s actions. A rapid ascent alone does not establish panic, and low gas does not establish that the diver ignored a gauge. Evaluate the data the actual equipment records and the explanations it cannot distinguish.

Regulator Failure

A regulator reduces cylinder pressure and delivers breathing gas on demand. Investigate reported free-flow, abnormal breathing resistance, intermediate-pressure changes, corrosion, and servicing history. Testing should distinguish observed defects from proposed causes and address manufacturing, maintenance, use, and postrecovery changes.

BCD Malfunction

A buoyancy-compensator malfunction can interfere with buoyancy control. Its effect depends on the malfunction, weighting, exposure suit, remaining gas, diver actions, and available assistance. Examine inflation and exhaust components under a documented protocol and compare the results with the recorded profile and medical evidence.

Tank Contamination

Suspected breathing-gas contamination requires sampling and laboratory analysis under a documented protocol. Preserve residual cylinder gas before refilling or emptying. Obtain compressor records, intake location, maintenance history, and applicable gas-quality specifications. Evaluate exposure and medical effects with qualified specialists rather than inferring them from a single symptom.

SCUBA evidence preservation

Preserve the recovered equipment, residual breathing gas, available dive-computer data, service records, fill-station records, and gas-quality certificates. Document emergency handling and later changes. Servicing can remove evidence of a fault, but it does not necessarily eliminate every means of investigating one.

Dive-Operator Negligence

Dive planning, briefings, supervision, and emergency response require examination alongside equipment and medical issues. Determine the operator’s role and the standards applicable to that operation.

Inadequate Briefings

Obtain the briefing content, site information, planned profile, buddy assignments, emergency procedures, and recall signals. Compare written materials, recordings, and witness accounts. Establish what information was available and communicated, and how any omission relates to the incident.

Buddy-System Failures

Review buddy assignments, separation procedures, training, and the divers’ actual positions. Separation can arise through several sequences. Establish the operator’s responsibilities and the evidence of each person’s actions before concluding that an assignment or supervision practice fell below an applicable standard.

Depth-Limit and Certification Violations

Depth recommendations and training requirements vary by agency, course, age, and activity. Obtain the applicable standards and the diver’s certification and experience records. A depth figure alone does not establish a breach or explain the injury.

Decompression Sickness: Causation and Medical Evidence

Decompression sickness involves injury associated with inert-gas bubbles during or after decompression. It can occur after a dive within prescribed computer or table limits; exceeding a limit is not a necessary condition. Divers Alert Network, Effective Use of Your Dive Computer. Evaluate the profile, gas, repetitive exposure, symptoms, examination, and competing diagnoses.

A dive computer estimates decompression status from a model and the inputs available to that device. It does not directly measure a diver’s tissue-gas loading or all individual risk factors. Divers Alert Network, Effective Use of Your Dive Computer. Preserve the device, settings, download method, and complete available history. A diving-medicine specialist should assess the clinical significance alongside medical records and treatment findings.

Training-Agency Standards as the Duty-of-Care Benchmark

Training-agency standards can inform the assessment of instruction and supervision. They do not exhaust the potentially applicable law or duties. Identify the activity, agency affiliation, course, standards edition, and any statutes, regulations, or contractual obligations relevant to the operator.

Identify the specific provision and explain why it applies. Compare the conduct with its requirements and consider other relevant evidence. Compliance or departure may inform the standard-of-care analysis, but neither independently resolves causation or liability.

Standards Reference: SCUBA Duty of Care

PADI, NAUI, and SSI standards define supervision ratios, depth limits, and briefing requirements. CGA Grade E specifies breathing-air purity. Recreational Scuba Training Council (RSTC) minimum standards provide a cross-agency baseline. Cite the specific standard and section, not ‘industry custom’ in the abstract.

Key Deposition Questions for Dive Operators and Instructors

  1. What training agency’s standards does your operation follow, and where are they written down?
  2. Walk me through your standard pre-dive briefing, point by point. What did you tell these divers on the day in question?
  3. How did you verify each customer’s certification level before the dive? Show me the records.
  4. What was the planned maximum depth and dive profile, and who set it?
  5. How were buddy teams assigned, and what did you tell divers to do if they became separated?
  6. What is your service schedule for rental regulators and BCDs, and who performs that service?
  7. Where do you source your breathing air, and when was it last tested to CGA Grade E?
  8. What is your emergency action plan, and when was it last rehearsed? Who was the designated rescue diver on scene?
  9. How many divers was each divemaster supervising on this dive?
  10. What oxygen and emergency equipment was on the boat, and was it functional?

Qualifications for the specific diving opinion

Instructor certification may support expertise in teaching and supervision. Equipment engineering, dive medicine, and other disputed questions may require different qualifications. Evaluate the expert’s training and experience against each proposed opinion rather than treating one credential as a test of credibility.

Expert selection should address qualifications, sufficient facts or data, reliable methods, and their application to the disputed facts. No combination of a certification, a log, and equipment testing guarantees admissibility. Federal Rule of Evidence 702, amended 2023.

The Autopsy in SCUBA Deaths

A suspected diving death warrants consultation with a forensic pathologist familiar with diving medicine. Coordinate imaging, dissection, sampling, and evidence preservation with the medical examiner. Interpret intravascular gas and other findings in light of recovery, resuscitation, decomposition, and the documented dive sequence.

Compare the autopsy with equipment findings, the dive profile, gas analysis, witness accounts, and medical history. A suspected gas embolism does not by itself distinguish panic, an equipment problem, breath-holding, or another sequence. State which findings support each explanation and which remain nonspecific.

Nitrogen Narcosis and Oxygen Toxicity

Nitrogen narcosis and oxygen toxicity are potential issues in a diving investigation. Assess the breathing mixture, depth, exposure duration, diver response, and medical evidence. A depth measurement or apparent mistake alone does not establish either condition.

Consider physiological impairment as one possible explanation for a diver’s actions, not as a replacement assumption for “diver error.” Evaluate the supporting evidence and the operator’s actual responsibilities for planning, gas selection, and supervision.

Rental-Equipment and Product-Liability Overlays

Rental equipment may raise maintenance, instruction, product-design, and supply questions. Identify who designed, owned, supplied, serviced, and used the item. More than one party or mechanism may have contributed, and the equipment examination must be assessed with the rest of the record.

Map custody and service history, including parts, modifications, bulletins, and recalls applicable to the model. Determine whether a relevant condition existed before the incident and how it could have affected performance. A recall or missed service alone does not establish causation.

Waivers, Releases, and Assumption of Risk in Diving

Obtain the signed waiver, transaction records, and circumstances of execution. Enforceability depends on the governing law, wording, parties, activity, and alleged conduct. Do not assume that a negligence label either defeats or establishes the defense; research the jurisdiction’s treatment of each claim.

Analyze assumption of risk separately from waiver and comparative fault. Identify the risk at issue, the participant’s knowledge, the relationship between the parties, and the governing doctrine. Whether an equipment or operating hazard falls within an accepted risk requires that analysis, not a general statement about diving.

Chapter 3

Pool, Spa & Aquatic Facility Drowning

Pool and spa investigations require assessment of access, physical conditions, operations, supervision, and response. Determine which regulations and standards applied and how any alleged departure relates to the injury.

How often this happens, and to whom

CDC reported 4,509 unintentional drowning deaths in the United States in 2022. CDC, Vital Signs, May 2024. National counts describe the public-health burden; they do not identify a mechanism or responsible party in an individual case.

CPSC’s 2025 report gives an annual average of 357 reported pool- or spa-related fatal drownings among children younger than fifteen for 2020 through 2022. It estimates an annual average of 6,300 emergency-department-treated nonfatal drowning injuries in that age group for 2022 through 2024. CPSC, 2025 Pool or Spa Submersion report. Keep the different reporting periods and fatal/nonfatal methods separate.

Population patterns can guide initial questions but cannot classify an individual death by age alone. Investigate the actual setting, access route, supervision, physical conditions, and sequence in each file.

The Premises-Liability Framework

A pool injury may raise premises, operational-negligence, product, or other claims. Identify each defendant’s role and the jurisdiction’s rules concerning entrant status and children. Duty, breach, causation, defenses, and damages require separate analysis.

Lifeguard supervision, and the standard the facility actually adopted

For a supervision claim, examine the governing law, the operator’s undertakings, and the training program in use. A private program may inform reasonable practice without supplying every applicable duty.

Jeff Ellis and Associates trains lifeguards to the 10/20 protection standard: scan the assigned zone in ten seconds, reach the person within twenty. The American Red Cross teaches a thirty second scan of the entire zone, including the bottom, and does not use 10/20. The Model Aquatic Health Code requires diagrammed zones of patron surveillance in which a lifeguard can view the whole assigned zone and reach its furthest extent within twenty seconds, and it declines to set any recognition time at all. The United States Lifesaving Association writes standards for open water and beaches, not pools. Chapter 7 works through the differences and the research on how lifeguards actually perform against them.

Obtain zone diagrams, certifications, training and audit records, staffing schedules, and time records. Investigate discrepancies between planned coverage and actual staffing. A missing diagram or expired credential requires explanation; it does not alone establish the surveillance conditions or the cause of a drowning.

Standards Reference: Lifeguard Supervision

Ellis and Associates 10/20 protection standard, and four hours of in-service training a month to maintain the license. American Red Cross: 30 second scan of the entire zone. Model Aquatic Health Code Section 6.3.3.1.1: diagrammed zones, whole zone viewable, 20 second reach, all water assigned. Section 6.3.3.1.2: no more than 60 continuous minutes of surveillance. Section 6.6.3.1, item 1: inadequate supervision and staffing is an imminent health hazard requiring correction or closure. Demand the surveillance audit records, certification files, in-service logs, zone diagrams, and the day-of staffing schedule.

Drain Entrapment and the Virginia Graeme Baker Act

Drain-related incidents may involve body suction, hair entanglement, mechanical entrapment, or other mechanisms. Identify the specific drain, cover, plumbing, pump settings, and contact evidence. The Virginia Graeme Baker Act’s additional-system requirement distinguishes a single main drain from an unblockable drain; apply the actual configuration and incident-date law.

Evaluate statutory compliance alongside the physical mechanism. Preserve cover specifications, installation records, flow ratings, pump and plumbing configuration, and any secondary system. A violation may be relevant evidence, but its legal effect and causal connection require separate analysis.

Chemical exposure and water-quality injuries

Chemical-exposure investigations may involve dosing, mixing, ventilation, contamination, and equipment operation. Identify the substances, concentrations, exposure route, and clinical findings. Do not infer the organism or chemical mechanism solely from a report of irritation or illness.

Obtain chemical readings, controller data, maintenance records, training records, and the incident timeline. Check the MAHC and other relevant guidance against the jurisdiction’s adopted requirements. Determine what each record measures and whether it reflects conditions during the exposure.

Visibility and rescue

Assess water clarity, illumination, glare, depth, viewing angle, surface disturbance, obstructions, and the victim’s position. Determine which visibility and lighting requirements applied at the time. A compliant reading at one location does not establish visibility throughout the pool.

Chapter 5 addresses clarity evidence and Chapter 6 addresses lighting and glare. Evaluate those conditions alongside surveillance, recognition, access, rescue, and medical factors rather than assigning visibility a presumed share of responsibility.

Bather load, crowding, and the water nobody is watching

Occupancy may affect sightlines, surface disturbance, surveillance demands, and water-treatment load. Compare the actual count and distribution of patrons with the venue’s design, staffing, and applicable occupancy requirements.

Admission counts, gate records, video, and staffing sheets may help estimate occupancy. Account for people who entered, left, or remained outside the water and for uncertainty in those records. Exceeding a relevant occupancy limit and causing a particular injury are separate propositions.

Evaluating defense arguments

‘The Drowning Was Instantaneous and Unpreventable’

A delayed response may be relevant to causation, but comparison with a response target is not sufficient by itself. Reconstruct recognition, access, recovery, and care. A qualified medical expert should assess whether an earlier feasible intervention could have altered the outcome, considering the mechanism and available evidence.

‘The Parent Was Responsible for Supervision’

Examine the responsibilities and actions of parents, facility staff, and other participants separately. Comparative-fault rules and the treatment of parental conduct vary by jurisdiction. Do not assume that lifeguard presence removes parental responsibilities or that parental inattention eliminates a facility’s duty.

‘The Victim Assumed the Risk’

Evaluate assumption of risk under the governing law and specific activity. Consider the participant’s knowledge, the visibility of the condition, and the defendant’s role. A general distinction between pools and open water does not determine the defense.

Hotel and resort pool investigation

For a hotel or resort pool incident, identify the owner, operator, manager, franchisor, maintenance contractor, and staffing provider. Establish each entity’s control and duties before selecting defendants. Review lifeguard requirements and representations, barriers, drains, water quality, lighting, warnings, and response records. Reconstruct the event and assess available insurance separately from the merits.

Facility records may support, contradict, or leave gaps in an allegation. Determine which records should have existed, who kept them, and why any are unavailable. Missing records alone do not prove the alleged condition or its causal role.

Barriers, Fencing, and the Attractive-Nuisance Doctrine

In an access-related child drowning, reconstruct how the child reached the water. Compare fences, gates, latches, doors, and other access routes with the requirements applicable to that property. Do not assume that every child drowning resulted from a barrier defect.

The jurisdiction’s rules for child entrants and artificial conditions require fact-specific analysis. Examine foreseeability, the child’s ability to appreciate the danger, control of the property, and available precautions. Prior gate complaints may bear on notice if they concern a relevant condition.

Signage, Depth Markings, and Diving Injuries

A shallow-water entry can cause head, spinal, or other injuries and may precede drowning. Examine depth, pool geometry, markings, warnings, the participant’s knowledge, and the manner of entry. Assess compliance and the likely effect of a proposed warning separately.

An open-and-obvious or assumption-of-risk defense requires the applicable law and evidence of the condition and participant’s knowledge. Deficient markings may matter, but they do not automatically defeat either defense.

Spa and Hot-Tub Hazards

Spa and hot-tub investigations may involve thermal exposure, medical conditions, alcohol or medication, chemical exposure, suction, and access. Establish the temperature, duration, equipment configuration, warnings, and medical findings before selecting a mechanism.

Compare the actual warnings and operating practices with applicable requirements. For a warning theory, investigate what information the user received and how a different warning could have affected the conduct at issue.

Applying the Model Aquatic Health Code

The CDC’s Model Aquatic Health Code addresses public aquatic-facility design and operation. Determine what the jurisdiction adopted and what remained guidance. Where a provision was not adopted, explain its relevance rather than treating it as an enforceable requirement.

Identify the jurisdiction, adopted edition, local amendments, and facility classification. Chart the relevant health, construction, and operational provisions alongside the evidence and any disputed questions about application.

Initial pool-investigation tasks

First ten steps in a public pool drowning

  • Send the preservation letter the day you are retained, naming video, logs, and the physical plant.
  • Identify every entity in the chain: owner, operator, management company, franchisor, maintenance contractor, and lifeguard staffing vendor.
  • Determine whether lifeguards were provided, promised, or required, and by what authority.
  • Pull the health code in force on the date of loss and the facility’s inspection history for three to five years.
  • Establish the water clarity condition before the pool was cleaned, using video, responder photographs, and inspection records.
  • Establish the light level and the sun position for the time of submersion, and demand the glare assessment.
  • Obtain the zone diagrams, certifications, in-service logs, audits, staffing schedule, and time clock data.
  • Verify drain cover compliance, barrier and gate condition, depth markings, and signage against the code.
  • Reconstruct the submersion timeline from timestamped records and compare it to the facility’s own response standard.
  • Map the corporate structure and the insurance before investing in a full workup.

Chapter 4

Public Pool Standards and Who Writes Them

Pool requirements may come from federal law, state or local regulation, adopted construction codes, and contractual undertakings. Model codes and private standards may also inform the analysis. Identify the authority and scope of each provision before applying it.

Distinguishing enforceable requirements from other evidence

An adopted health or construction provision and an applicable federal statute may be enforceable law. A model code, consensus standard, or private manual may have a different role unless incorporated into law or an undertaking. Departure from a private program is not automatically a legal breach; explain the duty, relevance, and evidence.

Ask three questions at intake. Which jurisdiction’s health code applied to this pool on the date of loss? Which model or consensus documents did that code adopt, in whole or in part? What did the operator promise, in its own manual, its franchise agreement, its insurance application, or its marketing?

Potential sources of pool requirements

Where a public pool’s duties come from
LayerExampleLegal weight
State or local health codeFlorida Administrative Code 64E-9; Texas Administrative Code Title 25, Chapter 265, Subchapter LLaw. Violation is a violation of a regulation.
Building and pool construction codeInternational Swimming Pool and Spa Code; Florida Building Code Chapter 454; California Building Code Section 3115BLaw where adopted, at the edition in force when the pool was built or altered.
Model codeCenters for Disease Control and Prevention Model Aquatic Health CodeBinding to the extent adopted. Otherwise assess its relevance and admissibility as guidance.
Consensus standardANSI/APSP/ICC-1 public pools; ANSI/PHTA/ICC-7 suction entrapmentMay inform reasonable practice or become binding through incorporation. Check scope and edition.
Federal lawVirginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act, 15 U.S.C. 8001 to 8008Law, enforced as a consumer product safety rule.
Private program the operator adoptedJeff Ellis and Associates International Lifeguard Training Program; the operator’s own manualEvidence of an undertaking or operating practice. Its legal effect requires the governing law and facts.

MAHC code language and annex explanation

The Model Aquatic Health Code (MAHC) is the national model for the design, construction, operation, and management of public aquatic facilities, published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The current version is the 5th Edition, posted in December 2024, with the annex revised in February 2025. It is not federal law. It becomes enforceable only where a state, local, territorial, or tribal jurisdiction adopts it, and jurisdictions adopt all of it, part of it, a modified version of it, or none of it.

The code volume contains proposed regulatory requirements. The annex supplies rationale and background. Cite the appropriate volume and section, and establish adoption before describing model language as an enforceable duty. An annex explanation may support technical reasoning without creating a separate requirement.

Verify the pin cite before you file

Section numbering has shifted between the 3rd, 4th, and 5th Editions of the Model Aquatic Health Code. Every section number in this book is drawn from the 5th Edition (2024). Confirm the number, the text, and whether the passage sits in the code or the annex against the published document for the edition in force on your date of loss, and attach the page to your expert’s report.

Identify the applicable edition and adoption history

Create a chart of the provisions in force at construction, alteration, and the incident. Check local amendments, transition periods, retrofit requirements, and grandfathering. A publication date alone does not establish when or how a jurisdiction made a provision applicable.

The consensus standards, and the name change that trips people up

The Association of Pool and Spa Professionals became the Pool and Hot Tub Alliance in 2019. Standards carry the designation in force when they were last approved, so the series reads inconsistently, and it should be cited inconsistently. ANSI/APSP/ICC-1 is still cited that way. Do not modernize the older designations.

American National Standards for pools and spas, current designations
DesignationSubject
ANSI/APSP/ICC-1 2014 (R2023)Public swimming pools: design, construction, installation, equipment
ANSI/PHTA/ICC-2 2026Public pool and spa operations and maintenance
ANSI/PHTA/ICC-7 2020Suction entrapment avoidance in pools, wading pools, spas, hot tubs, catch basins
ANSI/APSP/ICC-8 2005 (reaffirmed)Model barrier code, residential pools, spas, and hot tubs
ANSI/PHTA/ICC-11 2026Water quality in public pools and hot tubs or spas
ANSI/APSP/ICC-16 2017Suction outlet fitting assemblies, the drain cover product standard

Check each standard’s stated scope. Do not infer a lifeguard-staffing requirement or a public-pool barrier requirement from the title of a document addressing a different activity or facility type.

The International Swimming Pool and Spa Code renumbered lighting

The International Swimming Pool and Spa Code, published by the International Code Council, is adopted by many jurisdictions as the construction code for pools. In the 2024 edition, lighting is Section 322, with 322.2 requiring artificial lighting and 322.3 covering emergency illumination. In the 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2021 editions, the same material sat at Section 321. A 2019 incident in a jurisdiction on the 2018 edition is governed by 321, and a brief that cites 322 for it is citing a section that did not yet carry that number. The code does not contain a standalone water clarity section; water quality is handled by reference to the pool and spa water quality standard rather than by an independent turbidity test.

Trace the drain-cover standard through the statute and regulation

The Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act was enacted December 19, 2007, as Title XIV of the Energy Independence and Security Act, and is codified at 15 U.S.C. 8001 to 8008. Its requirements took effect one year after enactment. Section 8003(c) requires every public pool and spa to be equipped with anti-entrapment devices or systems, and requires a public pool or spa with a single main drain other than an unblockable drain to have at least one additional system: a safety vacuum release system that stops the pump or releases the vacuum when a blockage is detected, a suction limiting vent system, a gravity drainage system, an automatic pump shutoff, a device that disables the drain, or another system the Consumer Product Safety Commission finds equally effective.

The statute names ASME/ANSI A112.19.8 and provides for successor standards. Trace the applicable regulation, effective dates, product certification, and installation history. The date an opinion is written does not determine which product standard applied to an earlier installation or incident.

Drain-entrapment authorities and records

Review the Virginia Graeme Baker Act, 15 U.S.C. 8001 to 8008, and the applicable version of 16 C.F.R. 1450.3. Obtain the cover’s certification, flow rating, installation instructions, and manufacturer-specified service life. Document drain configuration and any secondary protection. Do not assume every cover has the same replacement interval.

What the states actually require

State and local requirements differ on water clarity, illumination, testing, and closure. The examples below require confirmation against the incident-date text, adopted construction code, and local amendments before use.

New York10 NYCRR 6-1.19(d)(2): a white and black object four inches in diameter, placed at any location on the bottom, must be clearly visible from the sides at all times.10 NYCRR 6-1.29: 30 foot-candles on the water surface where underwater lighting is provided, 50 foot-candles where it is not, underwater lighting not less than one half watt per square foot, and 50 foot-candles at deck level recommended for competition pools.

If the bottom is still not visible 48 hours after closure, the enforcing agent may order the pool drained.California Building Code Section 3115B: underwater and deck lighting must let lifeguards observe every part of the underwater area and surface without glare, night use requires underwater lighting with no blind spots, and if lighting is not operational the operator shall secure the pool and permit no use after dark.

Read each provision in context. A visual test and an instrument limit may address different aspects of compliance. Do not infer that a state has no lighting requirement from one repealed provision or one subsection; check construction codes, local rules, and other applicable law.

Nineteen conditions that require a pool to close

The MAHC identifies conditions calling for immediate correction or closure. The items below address supervision, visibility, lighting, equipment, and occupancy. Confirm the incident-date edition and adoption before describing them as binding duties.

Imminent health hazards relevant to detection and rescue

  • Failure to provide adequate supervision and staffing of the aquatic facility as prescribed in the code.
  • Failure to maintain an emergency lighting source.
  • Aquatic venue bottom not visible.
  • Absence of all required lifesaving equipment on the deck.
  • Number of bathers or patrons exceeds the theoretical peak occupancy.

Model Aquatic Health Code, 5th Edition, Section 6.6.3.1, items 1, 9, 11, 10, and 17. The remaining fourteen cover disinfectant residual, pH below 6.5 or above 8.0, filtration and disinfection operation, water supply, overhead wires and ungrounded receptacles within twenty feet, depth markings, cross connections, barriers, chemicals, broken or missing drain grates, broken glass, and a catch-all for any other public health hazard.

Separate the model closure language from the jurisdiction’s enforcement procedure. Establish the condition, the responsible person’s obligations, and any corrective action. A closure violation and a causal contribution to an injury remain distinct issues.

Who is qualified to run the pool

Operator credentials include the Certified Pool and Spa Operator and Aquatic Facility Operator programs. Verify the credential, curriculum, validity period, and jurisdictional requirement relevant to the incident. Do not treat possession of a credential as proof of compliant operation.

A credential does not establish what an individual learned, knew, or did. Obtain the relevant curriculum and training records, then compare the operator’s conduct with applicable requirements. Do not infer compliance or noncompliance from certification alone.

Build a standards chart

Standards chart for a public pool case

  • Name the jurisdiction and pull the health code sections in force on the date of loss, not the current ones.
  • Determine what model or consensus documents that code adopted, and at which edition.
  • Pull the construction code in force at the date of construction and at any substantial alteration.
  • Get the operator’s own manual, emergency action plan, and any private program it bought, and read what it promised itself.
  • Check the franchise agreement, brand standards, and insurance application for additional promises.
  • Confirm whether each provision you intend to cite is code language or explanatory rationale.
  • Chart every provision against the facility’s records: what the rule required, what the record shows, and where the record is missing.

For each potential departure, identify the authority, evidence, competing interpretation, and possible causal relevance. A standards chart organizes those questions; it does not resolve them.

Chapter 5

Water Clarity and the Failure to See the Bottom

Poor water clarity can impair recognition and search. Its contribution depends on the victim’s location, depth, contrast, light, surface conditions, surveillance, and response. Evaluate clarity as part of that sequence rather than assuming it caused the initial submersion or the eventual outcome.

What clarity means when a body is on the bottom

Submerged-object visibility depends on contrast, light transmission, depth, distance, surface disturbance, and viewing angle. A patron’s description of “clear” water does not substitute for the applicable visibility test. Record what the observer could see, from where, and under what conditions.

A 2022 study reported 108 manikin-detection trials involving four professional lifeguards at two pools and a mean detection time of 18.1 seconds. Vignac and colleagues, Ability of Lifeguards to Detect Submerged Manikins in Public Swimming Pool Environments. These results describe the tested guards and conditions, not the time a particular guard would have taken during an actual incident.

A Lifesaving Society field study reported difficulty detecting submerged manikins under some combinations of distance, depth, and pool finish. Before applying such findings, compare the study’s target, environment, observers, and methods with the incident conditions.

Visual tests and instrument measurements

Clarity requirements can include a visual test, an instrument limit, or both. The MAHC’s marker-tile provisions address bottom visibility under specified conditions. Identify the applicable provision, object, viewing position, and operating condition before assessing compliance.

State clarity tests differ in marker size, viewing location, and permitted methods. Florida also uses a numerical turbidity limit. Verify the incident-date requirement rather than treating a test described for one jurisdiction as a national rule.

Standards Reference: Water Clarity

Model Aquatic Health Code, 5th Edition, Section 5.7.6: bottom visible in static water whenever open; contrasting marker tile at the deepest point, four inches square, eight inches square over ten feet deep; visible from any deck point within thirty feet. Section 6.6.3.1, item 11: aquatic venue bottom not visible is an imminent health hazard requiring immediate correction or closure. Florida Administrative Code 64E-9.004: 0.5 nephelometric turbidity units and main drain visible. Texas Administrative Code 25 TAC 265.193(e): eight inch black disk. New York 10 NYCRR 6-1.19(d)(2): four inch object visible from the sides. California 22 CCR 65527: operator shall close the pool if the bottom at maximum depth is not visible from the deck.

Read the clarity provision together with the applicable correction or closure provision. Establish adoption, the condition at the relevant time, and the actions required. Citing both provisions does not itself prove that the operator violated either.

Why the water went cloudy

Investigate filtration, circulation, chemistry, bather load, and source-water or weather conditions. Records may support more than one contributor and may not document every change.

Potential causes of turbidity and relevant records
CauseMechanismRecords that show it
Filtration failureChanneled or exhausted media, torn grids, a bypassed valve, or a pump running below design flow leaves particles in circulation.Filter service and media replacement records, pressure gauge readings, backwash logs, pump repair invoices, flow meter readings.
Turnover shortfallInsufficient circulation can reduce particle removal; evaluate actual flow, filter performance, and incoming load together.Design turnover calculation, pump curve, flow readings, equipment substitution history.
Chemical imbalanceHigh pH or high calcium hardness precipitates cloudiness; low disinfectant allows algae and bacterial growth.Chemical logs, controller data, test kit records, chemical delivery invoices.
OverbathingBather load beyond the design capacity introduces organic material faster than the system removes it.Admission counts, gate receipts, camera footage, staffing sheets, theoretical peak occupancy calculation.
Source water or weatherFill water high in solids, storm runoff, wind-blown debris, or a nearby construction site.Weather records, fill records, maintenance notes, complaint logs.

Establish the duration and likely causes of any clarity problem. Compare maintenance history, notice, occupancy, and corrective actions. Do not infer deliberate disregard from cloudiness alone.

Proving the water was cloudy after it has been cleaned

Maintenance after an incident can change water clarity. Record what changed and compare later measurements with incident-time photographs, recordings, tests, and testimony. The following sources may assist that comparison.

  • Video with a known reference. Compare visible objects of known size and location. Camera exposure, compression, angle, glare, and lighting can affect their appearance; an indistinct drain in one frame is not by itself a calibrated clarity measurement.
  • Response photographs. Establish the capture time and any changes that occurred before each image. Do not assume a responder’s photograph predates all alterations.
  • Inspection records. Determine what the inspector observed and how close in time and condition the inspection was to the incident. An earlier citation may bear on notice but does not establish incident-time clarity.
  • Facility logs. Compare chemical readings, filter pressures, backwash records, and turbidity tests where available. Investigate missing entries without treating their absence as a measurement of water condition.
  • Witness testimony tied to an object. Do not ask a witness whether the water was cloudy. Ask whether they could see the bottom, the drain, the tile, the black line, and from where they were standing. The code’s test is the question to ask.
  • Search and recovery. Document search locations, viewpoints, methods, timing, and obstacles. Difficulty finding a person can have several causes and does not independently establish a clarity violation.

Interpreting a prolonged search

Assess clarity, lighting, glare, obstructions, search coverage, the person’s location, and uncertainty about when and where submersion occurred. A prolonged search does not force a choice between only two explanations or establish breach without further evidence.

Interpreting measurements and sightlines

Use measurements and sightline evidence together. Later instrument readings describe later conditions unless a reliable reconstruction connects them to the incident. Contemporaneous turbidity data also require attention to sampling location, method, and the viewing conditions relevant to detection.

Evaluating a clarity-related causation theory

For a theory that impaired clarity delayed rescue, investigate the following propositions separately. Evidence supporting one does not supply proof of the others.

  1. The water failed the applicable clarity test on the date of loss.
  2. The applicable code required closure, or at minimum required correction, in that condition, and the pool stayed open.
  3. The failure delayed detection. Reconstruct where the victim submerged, where the guards were, and what the sight line was, and show what the delay was.
  4. Assess whether an earlier feasible detection and intervention could have changed the outcome. Use qualified medical analysis and case-specific evidence rather than assigning the person a survival probability from a general table.

Drowning prognosis requires consideration of multiple factors. Submersion duration is relevant, but it does not determine an individual outcome by itself. AHA/AAP, 2024 focused update on resuscitation following drowning. State the timing uncertainty, medical findings, available intervention, and evidence supporting any opinion about preventability.

Testing competing clarity arguments

‘The water met the standard’

Ask which clarity test was performed, when, from which locations, and how it was recorded. If records are absent, investigate the testing and retention practices. Absence of documentation alone does not establish that a test was omitted or that the water failed it.

‘Cloudy water did not cause the death, the victim drowned before anyone could have helped’

Evaluate the claimed delay against the available medical and rescue evidence. A response target is an operational benchmark, not an individual survival deadline. Determine whether recognition was possible and what treatment could feasibly have begun earlier.

‘Nobody measured the turbidity, so the claim is speculation’

Assess clarity through the available records, images, testimony, and qualified reconstruction. If alteration or loss of evidence is alleged, examine the duty to preserve, timing, prejudice, and applicable spoliation rule. Routine remediation is not automatically proof of wrongdoing.

The case that changed a state’s rule

Marie Joseph drowned in a Fall River, Massachusetts, public pool in June 2011. Her body remained undiscovered for more than two days. State investigators reported poor visibility and concluded that the pool should not have opened that day. Associated Press, July 21, 2011. Attribute those findings to that investigation rather than treating them as a conclusion about other pool incidents.

The Marie Joseph investigation concerns a specific pool and sequence of events. Its findings may suggest questions about clarity, search, and closure, but they do not establish what another operator could see or what another jurisdiction required.

Clarity checklist

Water clarity workup

  • Identify the applicable clarity test: which object, what size, from where, at what distance.
  • Determine whether the jurisdiction places the closure duty on the operator or on the inspector.
  • Demand all video from the incident and the seven days before it, before the retention period runs.
  • Pull health inspection reports and citations for the three to five preceding years.
  • Obtain filtration, backwash, chemical, and turbidity records, and note every gap.
  • Photograph and measure the pool as it exists, including floor and wall finish color, depth profile, and the position of the marker tile or main drain.
  • Reconstruct sight lines from each lifeguard position to the location where the victim was found.
  • Distinguish detection time, travel time, extraction time, and the start of care. Compare each with any applicable requirement addressing that interval.
  • Ask every witness what they could see on the bottom, and from where.
  • Preserve the filter media and the pump settings before service.

Chapter 6

Lighting, Glare, and Night Operations

Lighting and glare can affect detection even when water meets a clarity requirement. Assess illumination, reflections, viewing position, target contrast, and surveillance together. The feasibility of reconstruction depends on how well the incident conditions can be established.

Three separate lighting duties, not one

Separate requirements for surface and deck lighting, underwater visibility, and emergency egress. Their scope and permitted alternatives vary by code and facility. Compliance with one requirement does not necessarily satisfy the others.

The numbers the model code sets

The Model Aquatic Health Code sets minimum maintained light levels for the water surface and deck: 30 horizontal foot-candles indoors at the water surface, 10 foot-candles outdoors at the water surface, and 10 foot-candles at the deck. Those minimums are drawn from the Illuminating Engineering Society recommended practice for sports and recreational area lighting at the recreational class of use. Where underwater lighting is provided, the code requires not less than eight initial rated lumens per square foot of pool water surface area, and it requires that the underwater lights, together with the overhead or deck lighting, be located so that all portions of the venue, including the bottom and the drains, may be readily seen. Deeper water calls for higher levels. Dimmable lighting is not permitted underwater.

Evaluate operating hours and floor visibility under the applicable lighting provisions. Those requirements may inform a night-visibility claim, but the analysis also needs incident-time conditions, surveillance, response, and medical evidence.

Standards Reference: Illumination

Model Aquatic Health Code, 5th Edition. Section 4.6.1.3: 30 foot-candles indoor water surface, 10 outdoor water surface, 10 deck. Section 4.6.1.4.2: lighting shall illuminate all parts of the floor to enable a lifeguard to determine whether a bather is on the floor. Section 4.6.1.5.1: underwater lighting not less than eight initial rated lumens per square foot. Section 4.6.1.5.2: no dimmable underwater lighting. Section 4.6.1.6.1: underwater lighting may be omitted outdoors only where maintained surface lighting reaches 15 foot-candles and the bottom and drains remain visible. Section 4.6.1.7.1: emergency egress lighting per the applicable building code. Section 5.6.1.1.2: the facility shall not be open if light levels are such that the main drain is not visible from poolside. Section 5.6.1.1.5: immediate closure for cracked lenses that are not intact. Section 6.6.3.1, item 9: failure to maintain an emergency lighting source is an imminent health hazard.

Lighting requirements during operation

Distinguish installation requirements from conditions for continued operation. Establish which provisions applied and what the staff could observe or measure that night. A visual check and a photometric requirement may both be relevant.

Ask who checked visibility, when the check occurred, how it was performed, and what action followed. Compare testimony with records. Do not infer that no check occurred merely because responsibility was poorly documented.

What the states require

JurisdictionSurface and deckUnderwater

A performance requirement addressing blind spots must be evaluated separately from a minimum illuminance value. Establish its applicability and the actual sightlines. A compliant reading at one point does not resolve visibility in another area.

Watts, lumens, and the retrofit problem

Watts measure electrical power; lumens measure light output. A historical incandescent assumption cannot be applied unchanged to every LED fixture. Review the adopted rule, approved design, and manufacturer’s photometric data rather than using a single conversion factor for all equipment.

An LED retrofit can change power consumption, light output, distribution, color, and glare. Determine whether the adopted code permits an equivalency and what documentation the approving authority required. Compare that compliance question with measured visibility under relevant conditions.

Glare and changing viewing conditions

Glare may come from sunlight, windows, deck fixtures, or other sources. Its effect changes with observer position, surface conditions, and light-source geometry. A later inspection may not reproduce the incident glare without accounting for those differences.

The MAHC addresses glare in design and operating provisions. Review requirements concerning windows, fixtures, assessment locations, and visibility during operation. Distinguish the code text from the annex’s explanation and determine which provisions the jurisdiction adopted.

Request any glare assessment and supporting records. Establish whether an applicable provision required an assessment, documentation, or both. A missing written assessment alone does not establish the visibility condition or the effect on recognition.

Glare-assessment records

Request sightline surveys, station-siting evaluations, operating-hour assessments, and records of adjustments to windows, blinds, and fixtures. Compare those materials with incident-time conditions and testimony about actual practices.

Measuring light after the fact

A lighting reconstruction requires evidence of the original fixtures, settings, condition, and environment. Document which variables can be reproduced, which have changed, and how those changes affect the comparison.

  1. Inventory the fixtures: type, lamp, wattage or lumen rating, age, and position, taken from the electrical drawings and verified on site.
  2. Establish what was working. Pull lamp replacement invoices, work orders, and inspection notes for the months before and after the incident, and look for lamps replaced immediately afterward.
  3. Measure with a calibrated illuminance meter at the water surface, on the deck, and at the lifeguard stations, on a grid, recording the meter, the calibration date, and the height and orientation of every reading.
  4. Match or account for fixture output, switching, water and surface conditions, weather, and solar azimuth and elevation. The same clock time alone does not establish equivalent light.
  5. Photograph and video from each lifeguard position, with a manikin or weighted target on the bottom where the victim was found, and record whether it can be seen.
  6. Compare the measured values to the code in force, and state which values are code, which are recommended practice, and which are your own measurements.

Photographs of a submerged target can illustrate a supported visibility analysis. Document camera settings, target properties, viewing position, and differences from the incident. A camera image does not necessarily reproduce human recognition or establish what a guard actually saw.

Why the underwater lights were off

Investigate why lights were not operating, if the evidence establishes that condition. Possible explanations include lamp failure, a disconnected fixture, a tripped protective device, timer settings, or maintenance. Work orders and testimony may distinguish among them without resolving the cause of the injury.

Have a qualified electrical expert assess the lighting installation under the applicable code and listing instructions. Repeated tripping warrants investigation of the device, circuit, and connected equipment. Do not assume that tripping proves current entered the water or reached the swimmer.

Night swims, rentals, and the pool that was closed on paper

For an after-hours incident, examine posted hours, barriers, locks, access records, permissions, and prior use. Establish what the operator knew and what duties the governing law imposed. A posted closing time alone does not resolve access control or liability.

Determine whether barriers and gates complied with applicable requirements and whether the operator knew of repeated unauthorized access. Analyze child-entry rules, notice, foreseeability, and comparative fault separately. Do not infer a duty or its scope from after-hours use alone.

Lighting checklist

Lighting and glare workup

  • Fix the exact time of submersion and compute sunset, twilight, and solar position for that date and location.
  • Identify the lighting code in force at construction and at any renovation, and the operating rule in force on the date of loss.
  • Obtain the electrical drawings, fixture schedule, lamp inventory, and photometric plan if one exists.
  • Pull every work order, invoice, and inspection note touching lighting for the twelve months before and three months after.
  • Ask who was assigned to verify that the main drain was visible from poolside before night operation, and get that record.
  • Demand the glare assessment from each lifeguard station, and the record of any adjustment made.
  • Measure illuminance on a grid with a calibrated meter, matching lamps, switching, and sun angle.
  • Shoot from each lifeguard position with a target on the bottom, lit as found and lit to code.
  • Check whether lamps were replaced or circuits repaired immediately after the incident, and preserve the removed parts.
  • Confirm ground-fault protection and bonding on the underwater lighting circuits, and read Chapter 8 before concluding the cause was ordinary drowning.

Chapter 7

Drowning Dynamics and Why Nobody Saw It

A person may submerge without immediate recognition by nearby people. Investigate the visible signs, viewing conditions, assigned responsibilities, attention, and response. The fact that a drowning went unnoticed does not by itself establish why recognition failed or who breached a duty.

Use precise clinical terminology

Drowning is respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid. Respiratory arrest can progress to cardiac arrest, and resuscitation addresses both breathing and circulation. AHA/AAP, 2024 focused update on resuscitation following drowning. Identify the clinical sequence supported by the evidence rather than assigning it a fixed duration.

Use fatal or nonfatal drowning and describe the actual clinical findings. Older labels can obscure whether respiratory impairment occurred and how symptoms developed. Do not use a terminology dispute or a universal time cutoff to exclude a diagnosis without medical review.

Clarify the medical opinion

Ask the witness to define the diagnosis, identify its clinical support, and explain alternatives. An older term alone neither invalidates the underlying analysis nor establishes a delayed causal relationship.

Observable signs and their limits

Descriptions of the instinctive drowning response include difficulty maintaining the airway above water, vertical posture, and arm movements directed toward support. These observations are not a universal sequence. Do not require shouting or conspicuous splashing before considering that a swimmer needed assistance.

Published descriptions of brief surface struggles should not be treated as a stopwatch for an individual incident. Establish what observers or recordings show and identify uncertainty about the start of respiratory impairment, loss of consciousness, and submersion.

Recognition, intrusion, distraction

The recognition, intrusion, and distraction framework provides categories for examining surveillance. It does not exhaust possible explanations for a missed incident. Compare each proposed failure with the actual assignments, sightlines, communications, and observations.

The MAHC addresses tasks and distractions that interfere with surveillance. Obtain the applicable text and the evidence of actual assignments and conduct. Evaluate how a proposed distraction affected observation in the incident, rather than treating its presence as a complete causal explanation.

What the research shows about detection

Detection studies can inform questions about surveillance performance. Compare their methods, settings, targets, and limitations before applying findings to the incident.

Measured detection of submerged manikins by working lifeguards
StudyDesignResultWeight
Brener and Oostman, World Waterpark Magazine, 2002More than 500 unannounced manikin drops at 90 United States pools and waterparks during normal operation, 2001Detected within 10 seconds in 9 percent of tests; within 30 seconds in 43 percent; over one minute in 41 percent; over three minutes in 14 percent; mean detection 1 minute 14 secondsTrade publication, no methods section, conducted at facilities audited by the firm reporting it. Widely cited, never peer reviewed.
Vignac and colleagues, International Journal of Aquatic Research and Education, 2022108 controlled trials, 4 professional lifeguards, 2 public pools, varying depth, distance, station, and bather loadMean 18.1 seconds; 64.6 percent within 15 seconds; 11.1 percent never detected within 2 minutes; shallow 9.70 seconds against deep 34.89 seconds; near 10.37 against far 30.21 secondsPeer reviewed and quantitative. Small number of guards and facilities.
Hunsucker and Davison, International Journal of Aquatic Research and Education, 2013289 facility inspections, 15,737 observations of lifeguard scanningAverage scan time 22.65 seconds; 41.9 percent of scans completed within 15 seconds; guards trained to a 10 second goal averaged 25.96 secondsPeer reviewed field data on scanning, not on detection of a victim.

The studies measure different tasks under different conditions. Scan duration, detection of a manikin, travel to a person, and initiation of care are not interchangeable. The findings do not support one multiplier for “ordinary” lifeguard performance or establish the time a particular victim would have been detected.

The 10/20 standard, what it is and what it is not

Jeff Ellis and Associates introduced the 10/20 protection standard in 1991, after development work its founder began in 1983. As the firm states it, a lifeguard should be able to scan the assigned zone in ten seconds and reach a person needing assistance within twenty. Published formulations vary on the second half between reaching the person and reaching the person and beginning care, and that variance is worth pinning down in deposition, because the difference is measurable. Ellis licenses lifeguards for one year, requires four hours of in-service training a month to keep the license, audits client facilities unannounced, and can annul a lifeguard’s license for failing a vigilance test or an audit.

A scan interval, recognition interval, and travel-time requirement describe different tasks. The MAHC’s zone requirements and the facility’s training program must be read in their own terms. Do not apply the Ellis 10/20 formulation to every facility or dismiss other relevant safety evidence solely because the facility used a different program.

Standards Reference: Surveillance

Ellis and Associates 10/20 protection standard, introduced 1991: scan the assigned zone in 10 seconds, reach the person within 20 seconds. Model Aquatic Health Code Section 6.3.3.1.1: diagrammed zones such that the lifeguard can view the entire zone and reach its furthest extent within 20 seconds, with all areas of the venue assigned to a zone. Section 6.3.3.1.2: no lifeguard conducts surveillance for more than 60 continuous minutes without an alternation of tasks. Section 6.3.4.3.4: no tasks that intrude on surveillance. Section 6.3.4.3.5: no telephones, texting devices, or music players. Section 6.3.4.6: remote monitoring systems may supplement staff but shall not replace them. American Red Cross: scan the entire zone within 30 seconds, including the bottom, middle, and surface.

Begin with the program the facility used, then examine governing law and other relevant evidence of reasonable practice. Distinguish a scan instruction from a recognition target and a travel-time requirement. Adoption of a program does not by itself resolve the full standard of care or causation.

The zone, the blind spot, and the empty chair

Examine the following potential surveillance problems against records, testimony, video, and site conditions. A single document may not establish how supervision actually occurred.

  • Zone planning. Obtain any required diagrams and investigate how staff assigned coverage. A missing plan may affect compliance analysis but does not alone establish that an area was unwatched.
  • Restricted sightlines. Document structures, features, glare, and other obstructions from the relevant positions. Account for changes since the incident before drawing conclusions from a later visit.
  • Water assigned to nobody. Boundaries between zones, and areas closed to swimming but still reachable, are the classic gaps.
  • Rotation and fatigue. Surveillance for more than sixty continuous minutes, missed breaks, doubled shifts, and rotations performed by leaving the water unwatched during the changeover.
  • Intrusion. The guard was testing chemicals, cleaning, checking wristbands, teaching a lesson, or running the slide dispatch.
  • Distraction. Telephones, conversation, and the supervisor who stopped to talk to the guard on the stand.
  • The empty chair. The facility advertised lifeguards and the stand was unstaffed, or staffed by an uncertified guard or one whose license had lapsed.

Building the submersion timeline

Build a timeline that distinguishes observed events, estimates, and unknown intervals. Use it with medical findings, physical conditions, and conduct evidence; chronological order alone does not establish causation.

  1. Last seen alive and above water, with the witness and the basis for the time.
  2. Submersion time or a supported range, identifying the observations and assumptions used. The recovery location alone may not establish where or when submersion began.
  3. Discovery, and by whom: a guard, a patron, or a body that surfaced or was stepped on.
  4. Extraction from the water.
  5. First rescue breath and first compression.
  6. The 911 call, which carries a dispatcher timestamp and often an audio record of the scene.
  7. Emergency medical services arrival, first documented rhythm, and transport.
  8. Arrival at the emergency department, with the first recorded temperature, blood gas, and neurological findings.

Compare timestamps and check clock offsets, missing footage, recording delays, and device accuracy. Record witness estimates with their basis and uncertainty. Do not assume that all estimates are wrong in the same direction.

Assessing the effect of delay

Submersion duration is a prognostic factor, not an individual outcome determination. AHA/AAP guidance calls for consideration of multiple factors when assessing children resuscitated after drowning. AHA/AAP, 2024 focused update on resuscitation following drowning. Evaluate the following evidence together.

Evidence relevant to an individualized outcome assessment
EvidenceQuestion to address
Submersion and respiratory impairmentWhat interval is supported, and how uncertain are its endpoints?
Injury and medical conditionWhat preceded immersion, what followed it, and what diagnoses remain plausible?
Rescue and resuscitationWhat care occurred, when, and what earlier intervention was feasible?
Environmental and individual factorsHow do temperature, exposure, flotation, and the person’s condition affect the proposed sequence?

Clinical basis: AHA/AAP, 2024 focused update on resuscitation following drowning. This framework does not assign a survival percentage to a particular person.

Separate observed timing from the counterfactual claim that earlier intervention would have changed the outcome. Explain the medical and operational basis for that claim and its uncertainty. Do not presume that delayed detection, rather than another event or several events together, was the relevant breach.

Detection systems and staff response

Obtain the detection system’s coverage, settings, alarm history, maintenance records, and staff-response procedures. Distinguish camera recording from active monitoring and automated detection. An alarm or a coverage gap requires context: establish whether it concerned the person, whether staff received it, and how it affected a feasible response. Check the applicable MAHC provision on supplemental monitoring and staff duties.

Detection checklist

Surveillance and detection workup

  • Identify the training program the facility adopted and obtain its manual, not a summary.
  • Get the zone coverage diagrams, or establish that none existed.
  • Obtain lifeguard certifications, license status, in-service training logs, and the audit file including vigilance test results.
  • Pull the staffing schedule, time clock records, rotation log, and hours worked in the preceding week.
  • Establish who was on which stand at the moment of submersion, and what each was doing.
  • Recreate the sight line from each stand to the position where the victim was found, at the same time of day.
  • Reconstruct the submersion timeline from timestamped records, and state the clock offsets.
  • Compare the actual detection interval to the facility’s own promised interval.
  • Obtain any drowning detection system data, alarm history, and coverage map.
  • Ask the operator whether patron surveillance was ever measured, and how.

Chapter 8

Electric-Shock Drowning (ESD)

Electrical exposure may contribute to a drowning without an obvious external injury. Evaluate that possibility through electrical, scene, witness, and medical evidence. Do not infer an electrical cause simply from the location near a dock.

Evaluating suspected electric-shock drowning

Electrical exposure can interfere with movement, breathing, or cardiac function. Its effects depend on current through the body, path, duration, frequency, and individual circumstances. An absence of burns does not resolve whether a relevant exposure occurred.

Water conductivity affects current distribution, but exposure also depends on the source, return path, voltage gradient, and swimmer’s position. Investigate suspected electrical involvement alongside other medical and physical explanations.

Information warranting electrical investigation

Reports of tingling, shocks, sudden loss of movement, or several affected swimmers near electrical equipment warrant investigation. Record the circumstances and consider other explanations. Absence of burns alone does not exclude electrical involvement.

AC Current Leakage in Marinas, Lakes, and Pools

Investigate dock wiring, connected vessels, shore-power cords, appliances, and other nearby electrical systems as potential sources. In pools, examine lighting and other relevant equipment rather than assuming the underwater light was responsible. Establish the fault and return path through qualified testing.

Separate the source of leakage from the responsibilities for detecting, interrupting, or warning of it. Determine which protective requirements applied to each system and whether the proposed protection would have operated under the incident conditions. A fault on a boat neither automatically absolves nor establishes liability for the marina.

NFPA 303: Marinas and Boatyards

NFPA 303 addresses marina and boatyard fire and electrical safety. Establish the edition, scope, and any adoption or undertaking relevant to the facility. Compare actual inspection and maintenance practices with the applicable provisions; the document’s title alone does not establish a breach.

Electrical-code scope and protective devices

Determine the relevant NEC article and edition for the installation, including marina, floating-structure, and pool provisions as appropriate. Distinguish personnel protection from equipment ground-fault protection. Trip thresholds, circuit coverage, and installation conditions matter; a protective-device requirement is not a guarantee that every possible shock injury will be prevented.

Obtain permits, drawings, inspections, modifications, device specifications, and test records. A qualified electrical expert should identify applicable requirements and evaluate any departure. Deferred maintenance may be relevant, but it does not establish the incident fault path or medical effect.

Standards Reference: ESD

NFPA 303: Fire Protection Standard for Marinas and Boatyards (operation, inspection, maintenance). NEC (NFPA 70) Article 555: marina/boatyard wiring and ground-fault protection; Article 553: floating dwelling units; Article 680: pool/spa equipotential bonding and grounding. ABYC standards govern the boats themselves; the American Boat & Yacht Council publishes electrical standards for onboard AC systems.

Testing and Detection: Electrical Expert Versus Aquatic Expert

Select expertise for the questions actually disputed. Electrical analysis may address the installation, fault path, voltage gradients, and protective devices. Aquatic-safety analysis may address access, conduct, and rescue. Medical or other specialized expertise may be needed for physiological effects and causation. Do not prescribe an exact number of experts for every case.
