Record connected equipment, loads, switching, water conditions, and changes before testing. Coordinate preservation with immediate hazard isolation and public safety. No inspection should require leaving an unsafe system energized or exposing a person to suspected current.

Coordination among specialists

Share relevant data among specialists and identify common assumptions. Each expert should assess the work relied upon within the expert’s competence and disclose limits or disagreements. EMT training alone does not establish qualification for every medical-causation opinion.

Evidence needed to evaluate an electrical theory

General recognition of electric-shock drowning does not establish that it occurred in a particular incident. A case-specific analysis requires evidence of the source, exposure conditions, sequence, medical findings, and relevant duties.

A later voltage measurement demonstrates the condition measured during that test. Explain how the test relates to the incident configuration and the swimmer’s possible exposure. It does not by itself prove that electrical current caused the death.

The Physiology of Electric Shock in Water

Describe the proposed physiological effect with attention to current path, magnitude, duration, and uncertainty. Do not assume a fixed progression from sensation to paralysis to cardiac arrest for every exposure. Qualified medical analysis should address the findings and competing mechanisms.

An electrical measurement and a medical conclusion address different propositions. Establish the evidence for exposure and then assess its likely effect in the documented sequence. Identify any inference that cannot be tested from the available record.

Water conductivity and exposure

Conductivity is one input in an electrical-exposure analysis. Salt water is not a reason to treat an energized-water hazard as safe, and fresh water alone does not prove a lethal exposure. Evaluate the actual circuit and the potential difference across the swimmer’s body.

Investigating the Suspected ESD Death

Preserve relevant electrical records and components while qualified personnel isolate hazards. Interview witnesses about shocks, movement, contact, and timing. Collect medical records and investigate other causes. Document changes needed for rescue or public safety before any controlled examination.

Boats, appliances, water levels, and electrical loads can change after an incident. Preserve evidence of those variables promptly. Weigh later tests against their differences from the incident rather than treating early measurement as a substitute for the other evidence.

Prevention Standards and the Marina’s Duty

Evaluate installation, protective devices, inspections, maintenance, access restrictions, and warnings as separate safety measures. Determine who controlled each measure and what the applicable requirements demanded. Assess the causal effect of an alleged omission rather than assuming that one measure would have prevented every outcome.

Chapter 9

Maritime & Admiralty Injury Cases

An injury involving navigable waters may raise maritime jurisdiction, choice-of-law, remedy, and procedural questions. Analyze them alongside the factual investigation. Location alone does not resolve every maritime-law issue.

Jurisdiction: Admiralty Versus State Tort Law

Federal admiralty jurisdiction over a tort requires two things: a location on navigable waters (or a land injury caused by a vessel on navigable water) and a connection to traditional maritime activity, meaning the incident had a potentially disruptive effect on maritime commerce and a substantial relationship to traditional maritime activity. That is the test refined in Jerome B. Grubart. When it is met, substantive maritime law applies even in state court under the saving-to-suitors clause.

Determine the substantive law and available forum separately. Maritime and state remedies can interact, as Yamaha v. Calhoun illustrates in Chapter 12. Analyze the activity, location, claimant’s status, and claim rather than assuming that every injury aboard a vessel receives identical treatment.

The Jones Act: Seaman Status and Its Implications

The Jones Act, 46 U.S.C. § 30104, provides an employment-negligence remedy for qualifying seamen. Under Chandris, the worker’s connection to a vessel or fleet in navigation must be substantial in duration and nature. The roughly 30 percent guideline is not a stand-alone eligibility test. Examine the worker’s duties, assignments, and relationship to the vessel.

The Jones Act seaman enjoys a plaintiff-friendly causation standard: the employer is liable if its negligence played any part, however slight, in producing the injury. The seaman also has maintenance and cure, a no-fault right to living expenses and medical care until maximum medical improvement, independent of any negligence claim.

Maritime worker remedies

Examine Jones Act eligibility under 46 U.S.C. § 30104 and the Chandris substantial-connection test. Separately analyze LHWCA status, situs, exclusions, and third-party remedies. Maintenance and cure and unseaworthiness raise additional requirements. The approximate 30 percent guideline is not a substitute for the full status analysis.

The Longshore and Harbor Workers’ Compensation Act

The LHWCA provides benefits for covered maritime workers subject to its status, location, and other requirements. Analyze employer immunity and any vessel-negligence claim separately, including special rules where roles overlap. A maritime job title alone does not establish coverage or a third-party cause of action.

Analyze employment status and covered location under the LHWCA, together with any seaman-status question. A worker’s inability to establish Jones Act status does not automatically establish LHWCA coverage. Check exclusions and other potentially applicable remedies.

Vessel-Owner Liability: The Unseaworthiness Doctrine

An unseaworthiness claim concerns whether the vessel, equipment, or crew was reasonably fit for the intended use. Distinguish that claim from Jones Act negligence and establish the claimant’s entitlement to invoke it. A condition may support an unseaworthiness theory without proof of notice, but the claimant must still establish the required causal connection.

Define the alleged unfit condition and the task at issue. Obtain appropriate technical evidence about the condition, its effects, and alternative explanations. An equipment defect alone does not resolve the entire claim.

Recreational-Boating Accidents

Recreational-boating investigations may address collision, wake exposure, propulsion contact, ejection, or submersion. Evaluate applicable navigation rules with speed, lookout, traffic, loading, weather, equipment, and participant conduct. A collision rule does not necessarily address every mechanism in a boating injury.

Propulsion-contact and ejection investigations may require design, guarding, cut-off-device, seating, and operating evidence. Select specialists for the actual issues. Preserve the vessel, records, and available electronic data before avoidable repair or transfer.

Cruise-Ship Injury Litigation

Obtain the passenger-ticket contract promptly and calendar notice, filing, and forum provisions. Research enforceability and statutory exceptions before concluding that a term bars a claim. Do not assume that every cruise contract uses identical periods or procedures.

For the substantive claim, identify the applicable duty and any notice requirement under the governing law. Analyze international carriage rules only if the voyage and jurisdiction make them relevant. Air-carriage conventions do not supply rules for a sea-carriage claim merely because the trip was international.

Cruise claim deadlines

Read the actual ticket contract and applicable law promptly. Identify notice, filing, and forum provisions and investigate enforceability and exceptions. Calendar the earliest potentially applicable deadlines while that analysis proceeds.

Expert-Witness Needs: Naval Architect Versus Safety Expert

Assign technical questions according to demonstrated expertise. Stability, structural condition, operating practice, navigation, human factors, and medical prognosis may require different specialists. Coordinate factual assumptions while preserving each expert’s independent analysis.

The Navigation Rules as a Standard of Care

Identify whether the Inland or International Navigation Rules applied to the location and operation. For any alleged violation, establish the facts and evaluate its relationship to the casualty. The applicability and scope of the Pennsylvania Rule require jurisdiction-specific legal analysis; do not treat any navigation violation as automatic liability.

Separate proof of a rule violation from its causal effect and any burden-shifting doctrine. Examine the conduct of all relevant vessels and the possibility of concurrent causes.

Limitation of Liability and Other Vessel-Owner Defenses

If a limitation action is available under the applicable statutory version, examine the vessel’s coverage, alleged negligence or unseaworthiness, and the owner’s privity or knowledge. Evaluate procedural orders, stipulations, and the saving-to-suitors issues before assuming that a limitation filing eliminates all jury-trial rights.

Review limitation procedures, claim deadlines, applicable orders, and any stipulations affecting other proceedings. Privity or knowledge is one question within that framework, not a substitute for statutory coverage or the underlying liability analysis.

Check current statutory coverage before applying historical limitation cases. Under 46 U.S.C. § 30502(b), the limitation chapter, except § 30526, does not apply to “covered small passenger vessels,” a defined category. Determine the vessel classification and applicable statutory version rather than assuming every rental or passenger vessel receives limitation protection. 46 U.S.C. §§ 30501, 30502 and 30526.

Passenger and Recreational-Boating Drownings

In an overboard or passenger drowning, examine the vessel event, entry into the water, injury, flotation, escape, rescue, and medical care. Determine the duties of each participant and evaluate possible concurrent causes. Do not frame the investigation as a forced choice between an unavoidable tragedy and one operational failure.

For cold-water exposure, establish temperature, duration, flotation, clothing, medical condition, and response opportunities. Assess whether a proposed earlier intervention was feasible and what evidence supports an effect on the outcome. General survival estimates do not establish that a particular person would have survived.

Chapter 10

Boating drownings, capsizing and entrapment

A passenger can enter the water because a boat overturns, fills with water, strikes another object, or throws the passenger from a seat. The Coast Guard records capsizing, flooding or swamping, collisions, and falls overboard as distinct incident categories. Those categories describe different events, not interchangeable explanations for a death. USCG, Recreational Boating Statistics 2024, incident tables and glossary.

Separate the vessel event from the injury mechanism

Build two timelines. The first should describe what happened to the vessel, including changes in direction, speed, loading, water entry and orientation. The second should describe each person's location, entry into the water, injuries, flotation, escape and recovery. Ask the retained experts to identify where the timelines connect and where the evidence remains incomplete.

Do not equate recovery from the water with a medical finding of drowning. In the Coast Guard's 2024 recreational-boating records, personal watercraft accounted for 38 deaths, of which 10 were drownings and 28 were attributed to other causes. That classification supports separate investigation of traumatic injury and submersion; it does not establish the mechanism in an individual case. USCG 2024, Table 24, p. 49.

Reported recreational-boating incidents, calendar year 2024
CategoryReported resultInterpretation limit
All reportable incidents3,887 incidents; 556 deaths; 2,170 injuries. USCG, p. 6Reported incidents are not a census of every injury on the water.
Capsizing202 incidents; 111 deaths, including 92 drownings. USCG, Table 16, p. 37The report defines capsizing as overturning a vessel. USCG, glossary
Person falls overboard239 incidents; 138 deaths, including 106 drownings. USCG, Table 16, p. 37Investigate why the person fell and what occurred afterward.
Personal watercraft38 deaths and 563 injuries. USCG, Table 24, p. 49This is a vessel category, not an additional incident category to add to the rows above.

These are 2024 figures, not estimates for 2026. The Coast Guard's index listed the 2025 report as pending when checked on September 30, 2026. USCG accident-statistics index. The 2024 report also describes changes in reporting policy, which counsel should examine before presenting year-to-year comparisons. USCG 2024, pp. 9 to 14.

Capsizing is not the same as flooding

The Ethan Allen overturned after a turn, waves and passenger movement acted on a vessel with insufficient stability. The Miss Majestic sank after water entered through a driveshaft-housing opening. These investigations illustrate why a reconstruction must identify both the initiating event and the vessel's response. NTSB, Ethan Allen investigation; NTSB, MSR-19/01.

Preserve the boat before a yard removes equipment, pumps compartments dry, repairs openings, or changes the load. If emergency or environmental conditions require alteration, document what responders changed, who changed it, and when. Ask a naval architect or qualified marine engineer to evaluate stability and loading. Ask a marine surveyor to document hull condition, openings, pumps and maintenance.

  • Loading: Obtain passenger positions, available passenger weights, fuel levels, equipment locations, capacity documents and departure photographs.
  • Vessel configuration: Record modifications to seating, roofs, rails, propulsion, batteries and permanently installed equipment.
  • Water entry: Photograph drains, plugs, through-hull fittings, ventilation openings, hatches, seals, damage and waterlines before testing.
  • Conditions: Obtain time-specific wind observations, forecasts, warnings, wave evidence, wake sources, routes and shelter locations.
  • Sequence: Distinguish the first heel or list from the first observed water entry and the eventual overturning or sinking.

Ethan Allen: stability after modification

On October 2, 2005, the Ethan Allen carried an operator and 47 passengers on Lake George, New York. During a right turn, the vessel encountered a wave or waves and rolled to port. Twenty passengers died. NTSB, DCA06MM001.

The NTSB attributed the capsizing to insufficient stability against the combined effects of waves, a sharp turn and the resulting passenger shift. Its postaccident calculations supported a permitted load of only 14 persons rather than the 48 aboard. The agency also identified the failure to reassess stability after modification as a contributing cause. NTSB, Ethan Allen probable-cause determination.

In a comparable investigation, obtain the original stability work and every subsequent modification record. Do not assume a displayed capacity figure describes the vessel in its incident configuration. Have the naval architect compare the actual configuration and load with the assumptions used for certification.

Miss Majestic: flooding followed by canopy entrapment

The amphibious passenger vessel Miss Majestic sank on Lake Hamilton, Arkansas, on May 1, 1999. Thirteen passengers died. The NTSB described water entering through a gap at the driveshaft housing after a clamp securing a watertight rubber boot was not secured. NTSB, MSR-19/01, Miss Majestic discussion.

As the stern settled, additional water entered over the transom. The continuous canopy trapped passengers and contributed to the loss of life. The investigation therefore addressed maintenance, flotation and escape, not just the initial leak. NTSB, MSR-19/01.

Keep those issues separate in discovery. Maintenance records address the opening through which water entered. Buoyancy and compartment records address how the vessel responded. Canopy dimensions, seat arrangements and escape openings address whether occupants could leave.

Stretch Duck 7: weather, flooding and restricted escape

Stretch Duck 7 sank on Table Rock Lake near Branson, Missouri, on July 19, 2018. Sixteen passengers and one crewmember died. The NTSB found that the operator continued waterborne tours after a severe thunderstorm warning and that waves entered through a non-weathertight bow air-intake hatch. NTSB, April 28, 2020 findings.

The NTSB also identified inadequate reserve buoyancy and impediments to escape. The fixed canopy and closed starboard curtain restricted passenger egress. Those findings concern the investigated vessel and casualty; they are not findings about every boat with a roof or side curtain. NTSB, Stretch Duck 7 findings.

Obtain the weather information available to each decision-maker, the time each warning arrived, and the authority to cancel a trip. Preserve the route, distance to safe exit points, communications, bilge-alarm data and onboard recordings. For escape analysis, document opening dimensions and obstructions with the vessel upright, flooded and in the final orientation established by the evidence.

Entrapment requires a specific mechanism

A canopy can block escape from a sinking passenger vessel. A personal-watercraft intake can entangle long hair, loose clothing or flotation-device straps. The NTSB and Yamaha describe these different hazards; neither supports treating every report that someone was “pulled under” as proof of a particular mechanism. NTSB, emergency-egress report; Yamaha, accident-prevention guidance.

Use “entrapment” as an issue to investigate until the evidence identifies what held the person. Preserve garments, hair evidence, straps, ropes, grates, handles, rails and relevant surfaces. Photograph contact marks and any material recovered from machinery. Do not demonstrate a suspected entrapment mechanism with a person exposed to operating propulsion equipment.

In re Aramark: the boat's limits and the weather forecast

On April 25, 2009, a rented Baja 202 Islander sank on Lake Powell and four adults died. The owner's manual identified the vessel as Design Category C and specified a maximum wind speed of 27 knots, approximately 31 miles per hour. The renters had not been informed of that classification. In re Aramark Sports and Entertainment Services, No. 14-4118, Tenth Circuit, August 1, 2016.

The appellate court distinguished two duties. It rejected a duty to obtain and provide weather forecasts in the circumstances before it, but recognized a duty to exercise reasonable care in warning renters about the boat's wind limitation. The court vacated the judgment and remanded without deciding whether Aramark breached that warning duty. Aramark, 2016 opinion.

Obtain the exact owner's manual and the rental briefing, not just a general weather report. Keep a vessel's design limits separate from an operator's cancellation policy and from any duty imposed by the applicable jurisdiction. A historical appellate ruling is not a universal rental policy.

Chapter 11

Jet-ski and personal-watercraft injuries

Personal watercraft combine propulsion, steering and rider support in a compact vessel. The NTSB's personal-watercraft study describes an inboard engine driving a water-jet pump, with a movable nozzle directing thrust. A propulsion investigation must distinguish that arrangement from an exposed outboard or stern-drive propeller. NTSB, Personal Watercraft Safety, SS-98/01.

Identify the craft before describing its operation

Record the manufacturer, model, model year, hull identification number, engine, pump, nozzle, intake grate, controls and software configuration. Obtain the manual that belongs to that vessel. Preserve the actual warning labels with photographs showing their placement, condition and visibility from each seat.

Do not apply a statement about a 1990s craft to every modern model. The 2013 Yamaha VXS/VXR manual describes an off-throttle steering system that supplies some thrust during specified deceleration conditions. Yamaha's RiDE system uses a separate lever to control deceleration and reverse thrust. Neither description establishes the equipment installed on another vessel. Yamaha, 2013 VXS/VXR manual; Yamaha, RiDE technical description.

Off-throttle steering and collision avoidance

The 1998 NTSB study described a recurring problem in the craft it examined: when an operator released the throttle, the reduction in jet thrust also reduced directional control while the craft continued moving. That historical finding warrants investigation of throttle input and steering response, but does not establish that every later craft has the same handling characteristics. NTSB, SS-98/01.

For the 2013 VXS/VXR, Yamaha states that its off-throttle steering assistance operates under specified conditions at planing speeds and does not function when the engine is off. Yamaha also warns that the craft has no separate braking system. The model's manual, not a generic account of “jet skis,” supplies those operational details. Yamaha, 2013 VXS/VXR manual, operating limitations and stopping.

Have a qualified reconstruction expert evaluate the approach speed, separation, sightlines, throttle history, steering input and time available. Do not infer speed solely from spray, engine sound or a witness's adjective. If testing is appropriate, use an agreed protocol, instrumented measurements and a representative exemplar rather than altering the evidence craft without notice.

Wake encounters and rider ejection

In Ford v. Polaris, a passenger fell backward from a personal watercraft and entered the high-pressure jet stream. The appellate opinion describes hand position, rear handholds, craft movement, and nozzle location. Each supplies detail for evaluating the ejection and injury sequence. Ford v. Polaris Industries, No. A106375, May 18, 2006.

Document the seating order and each rider's position before the event. Preserve evidence of acceleration, turns, wake direction, wake source, separation between craft, handholds and instructions to passengers. Reconstruct whether the rider separated from the seat before, during or after a collision. Do not use the existence of a wake alone to establish unsafe operation.

Water-jet injuries without an exposed propeller

A water jet can cause severe internal injury without blade contact. Yamaha's 2013 VXS/VXR manual warns that forceful water entry into the rectum or vagina can cause severe internal injury and that ordinary swimwear does not provide adequate protection. It directs riders to use a wetsuit bottom or equivalent protective clothing as defined in that manual. Yamaha, 2013 VXS/VXR manual, required protective equipment.

Ford v. Polaris documents a passenger's severe internal injuries after rearward ejection into the jet stream. Hickerson v. Yamaha also involved serious internal injuries, but the plaintiff's warning and design claims failed on the evidentiary record. The injury category does not decide whether a product was defective. Ford, 2006 opinion; Hickerson, Fourth Circuit, February 20, 2018.

Preserve the passenger's clothing, seat and nozzle geometry, warning labels, rental equipment lists and training materials. Obtain the treating physicians' operative findings and diagnostic images. Ask the medical expert and the propulsion expert to address their respective parts of the mechanism. Do not substitute an attorney's interpretation of photographs for medical causation testimony.

Intake entanglement and powered machinery

Yamaha warns that long hair, loose clothing and personal-flotation-device straps can entangle in moving parts and cause severe injury or drowning. Its guidance also warns against applying throttle when someone is standing or swimming near the rear of the craft. Yamaha, To Prevent Accidents.

Before anyone clears the intake, document the grate, fasteners, pump, shaft and any recovered material. Record who moved the craft and whether anyone ran the engine after recovery. Ask the examining expert to distinguish physical entanglement from jet exposure, hull contact and movement caused by waves or another vessel. Keep each explanation provisional until supported by evidence.

Engine cut-off devices and motion after ejection

An engine cut-off switch link connects an operator to a system intended to stop the engine when the operator separates from the operating position. Federal law requires use on covered recreational vessels while operating on plane or above displacement speed, subject to statutory exceptions. The statutory definition includes vessels under 26 feet capable of at least 115 pounds of static thrust. 46 U.S.C. § 4312.

The federal exceptions include an enclosed main helm and a vessel that lacks a switch and is not required to have one. State law and the vessel's own instructions require separate examination. Do not present the federal rule as an unconditional requirement for every vessel and every operating condition. 46 U.S.C. § 4312(b) and (c).

Preserve the switch, clip, cord, attachment point, wireless components if present, and photographs taken before disconnection. Record who wore or held the link. Examine whether the operator actually separated far enough to activate it. Preserve the as-found state before conducting a documented function test.

Continued movement does not by itself prove that an engine continued running. Yamaha warns that stopping the engine does not immediately stop the craft's forward motion. Distinguish engine sound, pump operation and powered acceleration from momentum, waves and current. Yamaha, PWC Controls.

Overturning, reboarding and rescue

The 2013 VXS/VXR manual specifies a particular righting direction and an engine-shutoff procedure for a capsized craft. Such instructions are model-specific. Do not copy one manufacturer's recovery procedure into an opinion about a different machine. Yamaha, 2013 VXS/VXR manual, capsized watercraft.

Reconstruct the interval from separation to recovery. Identify who remained with the vessel, where each person surfaced, the available flotation, communications and rescue equipment, and who first reached the injured person. Record attempted reboarding separately from rescue. Have the appropriate experts assess rescue feasibility from the actual conditions rather than a generic survival-time estimate.

Rental instruction must address the actual machine

New York Navigation Law § 73-a requires a livery operator or agent to explain and demonstrate operating procedures and safety equipment by video or an actual in-water demonstration. It then requires the user to demonstrate the ability to operate the craft and use its safety equipment. The statute also requires each rider to wear a securely fastened Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device. New York Navigation Law § 73-a(1)(a), (2)(b) and (2)(c).

The displayed statute prohibits rental to a user under 16 and contains a limited certificate exception for a person over 18 operating within specified supervised boundaries. Subsection (2)(f), which contains that exception, is marked for repeal on January 1, 2027. Verify the incident-date text, the user's circumstances and any other applicable provisions before forming a compliance opinion. New York Navigation Law § 73-a(2).

Request the actual briefing video, its version, the language used, the instructor's records and any recording of the renter's demonstration. Compare the script with the machine supplied. A signed acknowledgment is one item of evidence; investigate what the operator demonstrated and what the renter actually did.

Chapter 12

Decided watercraft cases and the limits of their holdings

A design-defect judgment, a preemption decision and a ruling about available damages answer different legal questions. Identify the question a court actually decided before using a case in an expert report or motion. The examples below identify the reported decision, not a promise that every later claim with similar injuries will receive the same treatment.

Ford v. Polaris: rearward ejection and jet-stream injury

Susan Ford suffered severe internal injuries on September 9, 2001, after falling from the rear of a Polaris SLH-700 on Lake Berryessa. The opinion describes her difficulty holding the rear grips and her exposure to the jet nozzle after she lost her hold. The jury found a design defect and causation. Ford v. Polaris Industries, California Court of Appeal, No. A106375, May 18, 2006.

The Court of Appeal affirmed. It held that primary assumption of risk did not bar the strict-products-liability design claim in the circumstances presented. The court distinguished ordinary risks of falling into the water from the particular risk of internal injury caused by rearward ejection into a high-pressure jet. Ford, 2006 opinion.

The jury did not reach the separate warning-defect theory. Do not cite Ford as a holding that every warning was inadequate or that every passenger's operator was negligent. For a design investigation, obtain the handhold configuration, seating geometry and evidence supporting any proposed alternative. Ford, jury findings and appellate analysis.

Hickerson v. Yamaha: injury severity does not replace admissible proof

Hickerson involved serious internal injuries during personal-watercraft use and claims based on warning and design defects. In 2018, the Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Yamaha. The court upheld the exclusion of the plaintiff's expert warning opinion and concluded that the record lacked admissible evidence supporting either defect theory. Hickerson v. Yamaha Motor Corporation, No. 17-1075, February 20, 2018.

This was a defense judgment on that record, not a finding that water-jet injuries cannot occur. Review the evidentiary basis for every proposed warning and alternative design before disclosure. Ask the retained expert to identify the method, supporting data, limitations and connection to the specific accident.

Truong v. Nguyen: collision and primary assumption of risk

Rachael Truong died when two personal watercraft collided at Coyote Lake, California, on June 1, 2003. She was a passenger on a Polaris SLX. The other vessel was a Yamaha WaveRunner GP1300R. Truong v. Nguyen, No. H029974, November 5, 2007.

The California Court of Appeal affirmed summary judgment for the defendants. It applied primary assumption of risk to personal-watercraft coparticipants, including passengers, and found no triable issue of intentional injury or conduct so reckless that it fell outside the ordinary activity. The negligent-entrustment claim also failed on the evidence presented. Truong, 2007 opinion.

Do not extend that California coparticipant analysis automatically to a commercial instructor, rental business, manufacturer or a claim governed by maritime law. Identify each defendant's relationship to the activity and the law that governs the claim. Preserve the route, traffic pattern, speed evidence, operator experience and opportunity to observe the other craft.

Yamaha v. Calhoun: a jet-ski death and available remedies

Twelve-year-old Natalie Calhoun died on July 6, 1989, after a rented Yamaha WaveJammer struck an anchored vessel in Puerto Rico's territorial waters. Her parents asserted product-liability claims and sought remedies under state wrongful-death and survival law. Yamaha Motor Corp., U.S.A. v. Calhoun, 516 U.S. 199 (1996).

The Supreme Court held that state remedies remained applicable in the circumstances presented, involving the death of a nonseafarer in territorial waters. The Court did not determine that Yamaha's product was defective. It also did not resolve every choice-of-law question or award the requested categories of damages. Calhoun, 516 U.S. 199.

Resolve the claimant's status, location and governing remedial law before valuing a claim. Keep that legal analysis separate from the engineering question of why the collision occurred. A remedies decision cannot establish defect or causation.

Cuenllas v. Yamaha: an off-throttle trial example

A 2010 article by engineer Craig Good describes an August 1997 collision involving rented Yamaha WaveRunner III craft in the Bahamas. According to the article, Burt Diaz released the throttle, attempted to steer around David Cuenllas, and struck him. Cuenllas suffered paraplegia. Craig Good, “Personal watercraft: High-speed fun, high-speed defects,” Plaintiff, August 2010.

The article identifies the proceeding as David Cuenllas v. Yamaha Motor Corporation, Los Angeles County Superior Court No. BC 196681, and reports a February 2000 verdict based on the failure to install a rudder. It describes testing of an alternative rudder arrangement. This account is a secondary litigation source, not the verdict form or an appellate opinion. Good, 2010 case account.

Obtain the trial record and later procedural history before relying on the reported outcome. For another craft, evaluate its actual steering system and a technically supported alternative. Do not transfer the article's test distances or results to a different model.

Sprietsma v. Mercury Marine: preemption is not a defect finding

Jeanne Sprietsma fell from a ski boat on July 10, 1995, and suffered fatal injuries from its outboard propeller. Her estate alleged that the motor was unreasonably dangerous because it lacked a propeller guard. Sprietsma v. Mercury Marine, 537 U.S. 51 (2002).

The Supreme Court held that the Federal Boat Safety Act and the Coast Guard's decision not to require propeller guards did not preempt the state common-law claim before it. The Court reversed and remanded. It expressly did not decide the merits or whether the claim was viable under Illinois law. Sprietsma, 537 U.S. 51.

Use Sprietsma for the preemption issue it decided. A proposed guard still requires analysis of the relevant product, feasible design, performance, risks and causal effect. The absence of a federal mandate is not a substitute for that analysis.

Brochtrup v. Mercury Marine: propeller contact during rope recovery

Jacob Brochtrup entered the water behind a Sea Ray ski boat to retrieve a tow rope. The operator put the boat into reverse and backed over him. The MerCruiser stern-drive propeller severely injured his right leg, which surgeons ultimately amputated at the hip. Brochtrup v. Mercury Marine, Fifth Circuit No. 10-50534, May 27, 2011.

The Fifth Circuit affirmed the judgment after a jury found a design defect. The court found sufficient evidence concerning an unreasonably dangerous design and a safer alternative. The opinion is unpublished and expressly limits its precedential effect under Fifth Circuit Rule 47.5. Brochtrup, 2011 opinion.

Preserve the control position, tow-rope arrangement, sightlines from the helm, communications and the injured person's entry location. Do not confuse this stern-drive propeller mechanism with a personal-watercraft jet pump. Any comparison must identify the actual machinery and supported contact sequence.

Authority and evidence status

These summaries distinguish court holdings, agency findings and secondary accounts. They do not supply a complete subsequent-history or citator review. Before filing, obtain the full authority, check later treatment and apply the incident-date law. NTSB findings are investigative determinations, not civil verdicts; counsel must separately evaluate admissibility.

Chapter 13

Ian Gumbs: reported facts and unresolved questions

ABC7 New York reported that Ian Gumbs, 56, died after an August 14 personal-watercraft incident involving a rental from Swan Marina NYC in Howard Beach, Queens. His wife, Stacey Thomas, was injured and filed a lawsuit alleging gross negligence. Kemberly Richardson, ABC7 New York, report available September 30, 2026.

What the public report states

ABC7 identifies Thomas as Gumbs's wife and reports that the couple rented a personal watercraft from Swan Marina NYC. It reports that they went out with an instructor while wearing life vests and that both entered the water during the incident. ABC7 states that Gumbs died at a hospital. ABC7, Gumbs report.

According to ABC7's account of the lawsuit, the instructor operated nearby and performed a maneuver that allegedly created turbulent wakes. The same report attributes to the lawsuit an allegation of a hole at the front of the craft with white foam visible around it. Thomas reportedly observed that condition after the craft was lifted from the water. ABC7, allegations attributed to the lawsuit.

Thomas described the craft's movement and her husband's movement in the water. ABC7 also reported an alleged postincident statement by the instructor. These are reported witness statements and allegations, not measurements, medical findings or judicial determinations. ABC7, Thomas interview and lawsuit account.

What the reporting does not establish

The ABC7 article does not identify the craft's make, model or model year. It does not provide a medical examiner's determination, a technical inspection, a reconstruction, a court ruling on liability, or a response from the marina. ABC7, Gumbs report.

The report uses propulsion terminology within Thomas's description but supplies no technical findings about the equipment or injury mechanism. ABC7, reported witness description. A technical reconstruction requires identification of the actual machinery and evidence of its operation.

Questions that require primary evidence

  • Vessel identity: What craft and other vessels were involved, and what propulsion and control systems did each have?
  • Sequence: What do original recordings, witness accounts and physical evidence establish about each vessel's route and each person's movement?
  • Condition: What was the craft's condition before departure, during the incident and after recovery? When did any documented damage occur?
  • Instruction: What instructions, demonstrations and equipment did the rental business provide? What records document them?
  • Controls: What evidence establishes the engine and control states at each relevant time? What was the as-found condition of any engine cut-off device?
  • Medical findings: What do the treating records, autopsy, imaging and other primary medical evidence establish about the injuries and death?
  • Response: Who observed, assisted, communicated with emergency services and recovered the participants? What reliable timestamps exist?
  • Other accounts: What do the instructor, marina, other witnesses and responding agencies report? What evidence supports or contradicts each account?

Primary records

The relevant records include filed pleadings and responses, agency reports, original recordings with metadata, medical records, vessel identification and recovery documentation. Rental records, instruction materials, maintenance documents and incident-date requirements provide the basis for evaluating the rental operation and the vessel's condition.

Chapter 14

Causation, Physics & the Science of Drowning

Causation analysis examines the relationships among the event, injury, conduct, and proposed safeguards. Medical, physical, operational, and legal questions require distinct support. More than one factor may contribute, and an incomplete record may prevent a confident allocation of their effects.

The Physiological Sequence of Drowning

Drowning involves respiratory impairment from immersion or submersion and can progress to cardiac arrest through hypoxia. AHA/AAP, 2024 focused update on resuscitation following drowning. The sequence and timing vary; reconstruct what the medical and scene evidence supports without assuming that every person experienced laryngospasm or the same progression.

Use the clinical findings and accepted drowning terminology rather than “wet,” “dry,” or “delayed” as explanations. Describe respiratory impairment, symptoms, treatment, and outcome. A label does not establish when an injury began or what caused later deterioration.

Fluid Dynamics: How Current, Depth, and Temperature Shape Outcomes

Evaluate current, depth, and temperature as separate physical inputs that may interact with injury and human response. A simplified drag calculation holds other variables constant; actual posture, projected area, and relative motion may differ. Cold exposure also requires individualized analysis rather than a universal temperature threshold or incapacitation clock.

Document how the expert derives current velocity, force, or heat-transfer estimates and how sensitive the result is to uncertain inputs. A force estimate alone does not establish what a particular person could resist or whether the defendant caused the exposure.

Time-to-incapacitation and response analysis

Time-to-incapacitation estimates are one part of the causation analysis. Compare the supported sequence with medical findings, injury mechanism, environmental conditions, flotation, recognition, access, and available treatment. Drowning prognosis requires consideration of multiple factors. AHA/AAP, 2024 focused update on resuscitation following drowning. A gap between a response target and actual recovery may inform the analysis, but does not by itself establish preventability or legal causation.

A pre-existing condition or sudden cardiac arrest does not by itself establish that prompt rescue and treatment would have been futile. Resuscitation guidance addresses cardiac arrest following drowning and emphasizes ventilation and circulation. AHA/AAP, 2024 focused update on resuscitation following drowning. Qualified medical analysis must assess the likely sequence, feasible intervention, and limits of any outcome opinion.

Autopsy findings and their limits

A forensic pathologist evaluates the circumstances, autopsy, medical history, toxicology, and other findings. Distinguish the diagnosis from the proposed sequence leading to death. Explain which findings are specific, nonspecific, or affected by recovery and resuscitation.

A drowning diagnosis does not by itself identify why the person entered or remained in the water. Compare medical findings with physical evidence of current, entrapment, electrical exposure, equipment condition, and other plausible mechanisms. Do not label a proposed mechanism “the negligence” before duty and breach have been established.

Coordinating physical and medical analysis

The medical and reconstruction experts may address complementary questions. Specify the qualifications and evidence supporting each opinion. The medical findings may constrain the physical reconstruction, while the reconstructed sequence may inform the medical differential; neither should be adjusted simply to match the other.

Share relevant evidence and make assumptions explicit. Experts should explain areas of agreement, disagreement, and uncertainty rather than treating consistency as proof. No occupational title or EMT credential alone establishes qualification for every question spanning those disciplines.

Integrating causation evidence

Separate observed facts from inferred mechanisms and legal conclusions. Identify supporting and contradictory evidence for each proposed cause, including possible concurrent causes. Explain the limits of the combined analysis.

Building a Causation Timeline for Trial

A trial timeline should identify the source and uncertainty of each event. Distinguish recorded times from estimates and show where events could overlap. Depict a proposed earlier intervention separately from the observed sequence so the demonstrative does not present a counterfactual as a fact.

Use timeline gaps to identify further investigative work. If a gap remains, disclose it and explain how it affects the opinion. Do not fill missing intervals with unsupported movements, physiological stages, or assumptions about what a person perceived.

The Instinctive Drowning Response

A swimmer in difficulty may be unable to call out or make conspicuous gestures. Do not impose a universal twenty-to-sixty-second sequence on a particular incident. Analyze the signs actually available to observers and the conditions affecting recognition.

The absence of an audible call does not establish either adequate supervision or an unpreventable death. Assess the duties, observations, positioning, and response of each relevant person. A general description of drowning behavior cannot assign fault among them.

Cold Water: Cold Shock, Swim Failure, and Hypothermia

Distinguish cold shock, loss of swimming ability, and hypothermia as potential effects of cold exposure. They need not occur in a fixed sequence or at the same time in every person. Evaluate water temperature, exposure, flotation, clothing, injury, and medical condition through appropriate expert analysis.

A cold-exposure model does not assign a legal duty or determine a person’s survival window. Compare the proposed physiological mechanism with warnings, equipment, access, rescue feasibility, and the governing responsibilities. State where the evidence cannot reliably distinguish among mechanisms.

Reading the Dive Computer and Other Data Logs

Electronic records can help reconstruct events, but their content depends on the device and configuration. Verify sampling intervals, settings, clock offsets, sensor accuracy, and missing data. A dive log may not record gas pressure; a vessel system may not preserve throttle history. Compare electronic records with physical and witness evidence.

Preserve original devices and data through a qualified examiner using a documented method. Identify overwrite risks and necessary power or storage precautions for the specific device. Do not assume that every download is complete or that later use necessarily erases every earlier record.

Explaining technical findings

Explain the reasoning in terms a non-specialist can follow. Use calculations, diagrams, or analogies only where they accurately represent the evidence and assumptions. A quantitative opinion is not inherently more reliable than a well-supported qualitative one.

Keep demonstratives within the support available for the underlying opinion. Identify uncertainty and illustrative elements. Clear presentation cannot cure an unsupported assumption or guarantee admissibility.

Chapter 15

Expert-Witness Strategy

Expert planning should identify the disputed questions, qualifications required, evidence needed, and disclosure obligations. Reassess those needs as the investigation develops.

Early consultation and preservation

Consult an appropriate expert early enough to identify evidence at risk and develop a testing plan. If equipment or the site has changed, document those changes and evaluate the remaining records. Delayed access may limit particular conclusions without foreclosing every reliable analysis.

An initial consultation can identify preservation priorities, plausible mechanisms, and missing information. It cannot be expected to resolve causation within a fixed hour or before essential evidence is available. Separate a preliminary feasibility assessment from a supported final opinion.

What to Send the Expert at Retention

Provide incident reports, medical records, photographs, recordings, operating records, environmental information, and access to relevant physical evidence. Ask the expert to identify gaps and priorities for the particular mechanism. Do not presume that one record is the most important in every case of that type.

Provide primary materials rather than only a preferred narrative. Ask the expert to identify missing evidence and contrary findings. Counsel should assess disclosure obligations, protections, and exceptions while preserving an accurate record of the work.

The Daubert/Frye Gatekeeping Challenge

In federal court, Rule 702 requires the proponent to establish the rule’s conditions more likely than not, including sufficient facts or data, reliable methods, and reliable application. Federal Rule of Evidence 702, amended 2023. Check the governing state rule separately; a recognized scientific field does not ensure that a particular opinion satisfies it.

Identify the basis for each opinion and show how the method applies to the available facts. Address uncertainty and reasonable alternatives. A calculation, published standard, or reproducible test may support an opinion without guaranteeing admission or excluding other methods.

Expert-opinion review

  • Identify the expert’s qualifications for each opinion.
  • State the facts, data, and assumptions relied upon.
  • Explain the method and its application to this event.
  • Show calculations where appropriate and disclose uncertainty.
  • Assess relevant competing and concurrent explanations.
  • Apply the forum’s evidentiary requirements.

Differentiating the Aquatic-Safety Expert from the Medical Expert

Define each expert’s scope by actual qualifications rather than title alone. Operational standards, electrical engineering, reconstruction, and medical causation may overlap, but each opinion needs adequate expertise and support. Identify the source of any specialist conclusion on which another expert relies.

State which findings each expert relies on and why that reliance is appropriate. Identify limits in the underlying work and disagreements that affect the opinion.

Questions for expert-deposition preparation

Prepare the expert to explain the opinion’s basis, limits, and response to contrary evidence. The following questions address common areas of inquiry without predicting the examination in every case.

  1. What are your qualifications to opine in this specific area, and have you ever done this in the real world (taught divers, guarded a beach, tested marina wiring)?
  2. What is your methodology, and where is it published or accepted?
  3. What materials did you review, and what did you NOT review?
  4. What facts are you assuming, and how does your opinion change if those assumptions are wrong?
  5. Isn’t it true that your reconstruction depends on estimates rather than measurements?
  6. Have you ruled out alternative causes, a pre-existing medical event, the victim’s own conduct, a third party?
  7. How much are you being paid, and what percentage of your income is from testifying?
  8. Have your opinions ever been excluded or limited by a court?
  9. Isn’t your opinion just as consistent with the defense’s theory as with the plaintiff’s?
  10. What would you have needed to see to reach the opposite conclusion, and did you look for it?

Preparation should reveal unsupported assumptions and genuine disagreements before testimony. Document the search for contrary evidence and explain how that evidence affected the conclusion. Confident delivery cannot substitute for a reliable analysis.

Video reconstruction and demonstrative evidence

A reconstruction or animation can clarify a supported sequence. Distinguish measured events from estimates and illustrative choices. Do not make an image more definite than the evidence, or assume that a demonstrative will be more persuasive than testimony.

Coordinating with Reconstructionists and Marine Surveyors

Identify the questions for reconstruction, marine condition, electrical systems, weather, human factors, and medicine. Share relevant data and reconcile inconsistent assumptions where the evidence permits. Preserve substantive disagreement rather than requiring specialists to adopt a single narrative.

Consulting Versus Testifying Experts

Consulting and testifying roles carry different discovery consequences. Define the intended role and investigate applicable protections and exceptions before designating the witness. A later designation may affect material generated during consulting work; the initial label does not guarantee continuing protection.

The 2010 amendments to the federal expert-discovery rules extended work-product protection to draft expert reports and most attorney-expert communications, easing but not eliminating the tension. Still assume the testifying expert’s file, data, and assumptions will be examined, and maintain the file with discipline. Make the consulting-to-testifying transition deliberate, documented, and with full awareness of its discovery consequences.

Selecting the Right Expert

Evaluate subject-specific experience, analytical methods, independence, and communication. The relevant combination depends on the questions to be answered. Prior courtroom experience may help assess fit, but it does not establish reliability in the new matter.

Review prior testimony, publications, and exclusion or limitation rulings in context. Determine whether a prior statement addressed comparable facts and assumptions. Do not select an expert for willingness to support a desired position or treat a prior admissibility record as a guarantee.

The Expert’s Report

An expert report should identify each opinion, its factual basis, methods, assumptions, and limitations. Explain the treatment of relevant alternatives and any remaining disagreement. Compliance with reporting requirements does not itself satisfy every admissibility condition. Federal Rule of Evidence 702, amended 2023.

Weak reports share recurring flaws: conclusions without shown reasoning, facts assumed rather than established, no consideration of alternatives, and overstatement beyond what the data support. Each is an opening for exclusion or impeachment. Fix them in the drafting, not at the hearing, another reason to engage the expert early enough to build the analysis properly rather than assemble it on the eve of disclosure.

Chapter 16

Damages & Case Value

Case valuation requires analysis of liability, causation, available damages, defenses, proof, litigation cost, and collectability. These considerations interact; none alone supplies a dependable value.

Wrongful-Death Damages: Maritime Versus State Court

Identify the applicable wrongful-death and survival remedies before developing the damages model. Available categories differ among state statutes and maritime regimes. Analyze DOHSA’s geographic and other coverage requirements and exceptions rather than treating every offshore death as identical.

Location, claimant status, claim type, and governing substantive law can affect damages. Forum choice does not automatically change the applicable substantive remedies. Evaluate damages with jurisdiction, procedural rights, and the merits.

Hedonic Damages in Aquatic Fatality Cases

Determine whether the jurisdiction permits recovery for lost enjoyment of life and how it classifies that loss. Separately research the admissibility of any proposed economic valuation method. Do not assume that a damages label or the victim’s age establishes a recoverable amount.

Economic-Loss Modeling for Young Victims

For a child without an earnings history, explain the data and assumptions used to estimate future economic loss. Address education, employment, work-life, consumption, growth, and discounting only as permitted by the governing law and supported by the record. Present uncertainty and sensitivity to competing assumptions.

For an adult, assess earnings, benefits, household services, work-life expectations, and relevant health or employment evidence. Avoid double counting and distinguish documented contributions from projected ones. The value depends on the evidence and permitted categories, not the existence of a category alone.

Structured-Settlement Considerations

Evaluate a structured settlement’s payment terms, costs, security, flexibility, tax treatment, and the beneficiary’s needs with qualified advisers. Check approval requirements for minors or protected persons under the governing law. Periodic payments do not guarantee an appropriate outcome for every beneficiary.

Using comparable verdicts and settlements

Compare reported outcomes only after identifying the claims, injuries, parties, jurisdiction, fault allocation, damages law, insurance, and procedural posture. Public reports may omit facts or combine categories. A large award in another case does not establish a likely result here.

Distinguish a verdict from a final judgment, settlement, or collected payment. Check post-trial rulings and appeals. Do not infer jurors’ reasons or assign a dollar effect to an expert’s performance without evidence.

Evidence supporting a valuation

Document the available proof for each recoverable category and the grounds for disputing it. Identify assumptions about liability, comparative fault, causation, and collectability. A technical reconstruction may inform those questions without resolving the amount of loss.

Use supported scenarios where uncertainties materially affect the valuation. Explain what evidence or legal ruling would change each scenario. Do not present a prior result as a formula for another injury or predict that jurors will accept a proposed number because they accepted a causation theory.

Categories of Recoverable Damages

Start a damages presentation by cataloging the recoverable categories under the governing law, which varies dramatically between state wrongful-death statutes, general maritime law, and DOHSA. The typical categories: the survivors’ pecuniary losses (lost financial support and the value of lost household services); loss of society, companionship, guidance, and consortium (broadly available in many states, restricted or barred under DOHSA); the decedent’s pre-death conscious pain and suffering (recoverable through survival claims where the evidence supports awareness); funeral and medical expenses; and, where the conduct warrants and the law allows, punitive damages. Chart which categories the governing law permits before building the proof, because effort spent on a barred category is wasted.

A claim for pre-death conscious suffering requires evidence supporting awareness and the relevant interval under the governing law. A general drowning sequence does not establish consciousness, experience, or duration for a particular person. Compare observations with medical findings and competing explanations.

Proving Non-Economic Loss

Where recoverable, relationship loss and conscious suffering require evidence specific to the people and claim. Use testimony, records, and qualified medical analysis as appropriate. Do not assume terror, awareness, or preventability from the manner of death alone.

Present the human-loss evidence without using it to supply missing liability or causation proof. Assess each damages category independently and account for legal restrictions, evidentiary disputes, and potential duplication.

Insurance, Corporate Structure, and Collectability

Identify the responsible entities, insurance, exclusions, limits, endorsements, and other available assets. Coverage and collectability affect practical recovery but do not establish an entity’s legal responsibility. Distinguish a potential source of payment from a supported claim against that party.

Consider recoverable damages and collectability with the merits, investigation costs, and client’s objectives. Limited coverage or a disputed causal theory may affect the assessment without supplying a universal accept-or-decline rule.

Chapter 17

Discovery Checklist & Deposition Outlines

Adapt discovery to the alleged mechanisms, competing explanations, and governing rules. Seek evidence of actual conditions and conduct, including evidence inconsistent with the requesting party’s theory.

Plaintiff Discovery Checklist

  • Facility records: operating permits, licenses, health-department inspection reports, and any citations or notices of violation for the three to five years preceding the incident.
  • Maintenance logs: pool chemical and pH logs; filtration and pump-service records; drain-cover specifications and installation records (Virginia Graeme Baker compliance); marina electrical-inspection and repair records; vessel maintenance and repair history; dive-equipment service records.
  • Incident reports: the report for this incident and all prior incident and near-miss reports at the facility.
  • Employee and training records: certifications (lifeguard, divemaster, captain, pool operator), in-service training logs, disciplinary records, and the staffing schedule for the day of the incident.
  • Prior incidents: all prior drownings, injuries, rescues, shocks, or equipment failures at the facility or involving the operator.
  • Surveillance video and photographs: all camera footage (secure before overwrite), and all photographs taken by staff, responders, or witnesses.
  • Physical evidence: the dive gear, the residual gas sample, the vessel, the drain assembly, or the wiring, preserved unaltered for inspection and testing.
  • Policies and procedures: emergency action plan, supervision/surveillance policy, safety manuals, and the operator’s adopted industry standards (PADI/NAUI, Ellis, USLA, NFPA 303).
  • Data logs: dive-computer download; GPS and engine-data logs for vessels; chemical-controller data.
  • Insurance: all applicable liability policies, declarations pages, and reservation-of-rights or coverage-position letters.
  • Corporate structure: ownership, management, franchise, and maintenance-contractor agreements identifying who owned, operated, and controlled the facility.
  • Weather and environmental data: water temperature, current, tide, and weather for the time of the incident.

Pool Visibility, Lighting, and Supervision Discovery

For a pool incident involving recognition or rescue, supplement the general requests with the following subjects. The list does not exhaust other issues such as medical events, access, or equipment failure.

  • Water clarity: the clarity test the facility performed, who performed it, and where it was recorded; turbidity readings; the location, size, and color of the marker tile or main drain used for the test; filtration, backwash, and media replacement records; flow rates and the turnover calculation; algae and cloudy water complaints for the season.
  • Lighting: electrical drawings and fixture schedule; lamp type, rating, and inventory; photometric design documents; lamp and lens replacement records for twelve months before and three months after; work orders on underwater lighting circuits; ground-fault tripping history; timer and automation settings; the record of who verified that the main drain was visible from poolside before night operation.
  • Glare: the glare assessment from each lifeguard station, any sight line survey, and records of adjustments to windows, blinds, shades, or fixture aim.
  • Surveillance: zone coverage diagrams; the safety plan and staffing plan; rotation schedule and break log; time clock records and hours worked in the preceding week; lifeguard certification, license, and audit files; vigilance test results; in-service training logs; disciplinary records.
  • Occupancy: the theoretical peak occupancy calculation; admission counts, gate receipts, wristband sales, and key card logs for the day; camera footage showing bather load.
  • Detection systems: any computer-aided drowning detection system, with alarm history, coverage map, calibration and maintenance records, and any alarms silenced, disabled, or overridden.
  • Barriers and access: fence and gate specifications, self-latching hardware, inspection and repair records, key card or fob access logs, posted hours, and any record of after-hours use.
  • Regulatory file: health department inspection reports and citations for three to five years; the plan review and construction approvals; the operating permit; any closure orders.
  • Standards adopted: the lifeguard training program manual, the operator’s own policy manual, brand or franchise standards, the emergency action plan, and the insurance application describing safety practices.
  • The scene, unaltered: written demand that the pool finish, lighting, fixtures, filtration configuration, and lifeguard stand positions remain as they were pending inspection, with notice before any change.

Defense Discovery Checklist

  • Decedent’s history: certifications, training, and dive/boating experience logs; prior aquatic activity and skill level.
  • Medical records: complete pre-incident medical history, including cardiac history, seizure disorders, medications, and any condition (e.g., patent foramen ovale) relevant to a competing cause.
  • Toxicology: blood alcohol and drug screening from the autopsy.
  • Victim’s conduct: witness accounts of the victim’s actions, rule violations, or disregard of warnings and briefings.
  • Comparative fault: evidence of parental or companion supervision (in child cases), buddy conduct, or third-party fault.
  • Warnings and instructions: proof of signage, briefings, waivers, and releases the victim received or signed.
  • Expert materials: Request the opinions, facts, data, compensation, and other materials discoverable under the governing rules. Account for protections and exceptions affecting drafts and attorney communications.
  • Damages discovery: the decedent’s earnings, tax returns, employment records, and the survivors’ actual dependency and relationship.
  • Alternative-cause evidence: environmental conditions, equipment provenance (third-party gear or boats), and any intervening act.
  • Prior claims: the plaintiff’s and beneficiaries’ litigation and claims history.

Deposition Outline: Dive Operator

  1. Business structure, ownership, and your role and certifications.
  2. Training-agency affiliation (PADI/NAUI/SSI) and the written standards you follow.
  3. The specific dive: site, planned depth, profile, and who planned it.
  4. Customer intake: how you verified certification and experience for this diver.
  5. The briefing: content, who gave it, and what these divers were told.
  6. Buddy assignments and your separation protocol.
  7. Supervision: divemaster-to-diver ratio and who was watching this diver.
  8. Equipment: source of rental gear, service schedule, and service records.
  9. Breathing air: source, compressor maintenance, and last CGA Grade E test.
  10. Emergency action plan: contents, rehearsal, on-board oxygen and rescue equipment, and what happened after the diver was reported missing.
  11. Post-incident: preservation of gear, notifications, and internal review.

Deposition Outline: Lifeguard

  1. Certification, license status, expiration, and which program trained you.
  2. In-service training: hours per month, who ran it, and what was covered.
  3. The surveillance standard you were taught, in your own words, and the response time it promised.
  4. Your zone that day: where it began and ended, and whether you ever saw a written zone diagram.
  5. Where you were positioned, standing or seated, and your scanning pattern including the bottom.
  6. Hours worked that day and that week, your last break, and when you last rotated.
  7. What you were doing in the two minutes before the victim was found.
  8. What you could see on the bottom of the deep end from your position, and whether anything blocked or reflected your view.
  9. Whether you were wearing sunglasses, and whether the sun or a window put glare on the water.
  10. Whether you had a telephone, radio, or music player on your person or at the stand.
  11. Whether you had ever been told to close or clear the pool for cloudy water or for failed lights, and by whom.
  12. How the victim was found, by whom, and what you did next, minute by minute.

Deposition Outline: Aquatic Facility Manager or Lifeguard Supervisor

  1. Your role, credentials, and who you report to in the corporate structure.
  2. Which health code governed this facility, and which edition you operated under.
  3. Which lifeguard training program the facility adopted, when, and what it obligated the facility to do.
  4. The zone coverage diagrams: who drew them, when, and how they were validated against the twenty second reach.
  5. How you determined the number of guards on duty at any hour, and what governed that decision.
  6. The theoretical peak occupancy of this venue, who calculated it, and how it was enforced.
  7. The water clarity test: what object, what size, from where, how often, and where the result was recorded.
  8. Your written rule for closing the pool for cloudy water, and every time it was used in the last three seasons.
  9. Night operation: the required light levels, who verified them, and the check that the main drain was visible from poolside.
  10. The glare assessment from each lifeguard station: who performed it, when, and what was changed as a result.
  11. Audits and vigilance tests: results, failures, corrective action, and who received the reports.
  12. Prior incidents, near misses, rescues, and complaints about clarity, lighting, or supervision.
  13. The emergency action plan: contents, rehearsal frequency, and how it performed that day.
  14. What changed at the facility after this incident, and when.

Deposition Outline: Certified Pool Operator or Maintenance Contractor

  1. Certification held, issuing body, date, and expiration.
  2. Scope of your responsibility under the contract, and what the facility retained.
  3. The filtration system: design turnover, actual flow, filter type, media age, and service interval.
  4. Backwash practice: trigger, frequency, and where it was logged.
  5. Chemical testing that day: who tested, when, the readings, and the controller’s state.
  6. Every time in the last three seasons the water was cloudy, and what you did about it.
  7. Who had authority to close the pool, and whether you ever recommended closure.
  8. Drain covers: make, model, certification, installation date, service life, and single or dual drain plumbing.
  9. Underwater lighting: fixtures, lamps replaced, circuits disabled, and any ground-fault tripping.
  10. What records you kept, what the contract required you to keep, and what is missing.

Deposition Outline: Marina / Boat Operator

  1. Ownership, management, and your responsibility for the electrical system (marina) or the vessel (operator).
  2. Electrical system: age, installation, NEC edition applied, and ground-fault protection present.
  3. Inspection history under NFPA 303 and any deficiencies found or deferred.
  4. Knowledge of ESD as a hazard and any warnings or swimming policies near docks.
  5. For vessels: maintenance history, safety equipment, and the operator’s certification and experience.
  6. The incident: conditions, who was plugged in, what was energized, and what was done afterward.
  7. Prior shocks, tingling complaints, or electrical faults reported at the marina.
  8. Repairs made after the incident (and preservation of the pre-repair condition).
  9. Compliance with the navigation rules (for collision/operation cases).
  10. Insurance and corporate structure.

Deposition Outline: Opposing Expert Witness

  1. Qualifications, real-world experience, and any gaps (never taught, never tested, never dived).
  2. Complete list of materials reviewed, and materials available but NOT reviewed.
  3. Every assumption underlying the opinion and the effect if each assumption is wrong.
  4. Methodology: is it published, peer-reviewed, generally accepted, or invented for this case?
  5. Which measurements and estimates support the reconstruction, what uncertainty applies, and how does the result change across supported ranges?
  6. Which alternative or concurrent causes were considered, and what evidence supports, limits, or excludes each?
  7. Prior testimony, publications, and any court that has excluded or limited the opinion.
  8. Compensation and the percentage of income from litigation.
  9. Each specific opinion, pinned down, with the factual basis for each.
  10. What evidence, if it existed, would change the opinion, and whether the expert looked for it.

Watercraft and jet-ski evidence preservation

Coordinate vessel preservation with qualified marine and propulsion experts. Address immediate safety and environmental needs while documenting any unavoidable change to the evidence. Use a written inspection protocol before destructive testing or disassembly.

  • Craft and components: Preserve the complete vessel, keys, lanyards, cut-off switches, intake grate, jet pump or propeller, steering controls, reverse gate, seats, straps and handholds.
  • Electronic records: Preserve available engine-control, navigation, rental-platform, GPS, camera and phone data. Have an appropriately qualified examiner determine what the specific equipment records before promising a speed or throttle history.
  • Configuration: Obtain hull and engine identification, build records, manuals, modifications, service bulletins, applicable recalls and preincident photographs.
  • Rental transaction: Obtain reservations, agreements, waivers, payment records, staff assignments, briefing videos, translated instructions, renter demonstrations and equipment-issuance records.
  • People and equipment: Preserve clothing, flotation devices, damaged straps, rescue gear, medical photographs and chain-of-custody records.
  • Route and conditions: Obtain original weather warnings, observed conditions, tide and current records where relevant, route restrictions, wake sources and available shore or vessel recordings.
  • Response: Obtain emergency-call audio, dispatch records, responder video, rescue timelines, communications and recovery photographs.
  • Condition changes: Identify every person who recovered, transported, stored, cleaned, serviced, tested or operated the vessel after the event.

Deposition outline: personal-watercraft rental operator or instructor

  1. Identify the vessel supplied, its model-specific controls, and the documents used to train staff.
  2. Describe the predeparture inspection and identify the person who performed it.
  3. Identify unresolved complaints, repairs, incidents or operating restrictions for that craft.
  4. State the renter's reported experience and explain how the business assessed operating ability.
  5. Describe each instruction and demonstration, including passenger position, propulsion hazards, steering, stopping and engine cut-off use.
  6. Identify the clothing and flotation instructions given to each rider and the equipment actually supplied.
  7. Describe the route, permitted operating area, supervision method, spacing rules and weather cancellation authority.
  8. Identify the instructor's location and actions at each time supported by the evidence, without assuming the disputed sequence.
  9. Describe the response after the incident, including engine shutdown, communications, recovery and medical assistance.
  10. Identify the craft's postincident custodians and every alteration or test.

Deposition outline: manufacturer or design witness

  1. Identify the model's propulsion, steering-assist, deceleration and operator-separation systems.
  2. Explain the operating conditions under which each system provides assistance and those under which it does not.
  3. Identify the design requirements and tests for rider retention, passenger handholds and rearward ejection.
  4. Identify the warnings and protective-clothing instructions applicable to the incident model and market.
  5. Identify substantially similar incidents and explain the criteria used to assess similarity.
  6. Describe any tested alternative design, including feasibility, performance, failure modes and unintended risks.
  7. Identify design changes, their dates and stated reasons, subject to counsel's analysis of discovery and admissibility.
  8. Explain which electronic data the actual equipment can preserve and what cannot be recovered.

Deposition outline: capsizing, flooding and escape

  1. Identify the certified configuration and each subsequent structural or equipment modification.
  2. Identify the passenger-load assumptions and any later stability evaluation.
  3. Describe passenger positions, fuel, cargo and equipment at departure and immediately before the casualty.
  4. Identify every potential water-entry opening and its as-found condition.
  5. Identify bilge-pump, alarm, watertight-compartment and flotation records.
  6. Describe the weather information received and each decision to depart, continue, turn back or seek shelter.
  7. Identify escape openings, covers, curtains, latches and instructions in the actual vessel configuration.
  8. Distinguish the witness's direct observations from assumptions about how the vessel flooded or overturned.

Using the Checklists and Outlines

Tailor the outlines to each witness’s role and knowledge. Follow up on factual detail, inconsistent accounts, and the basis for any statement about a standard. Separate direct observation from inference or information supplied by others.

Establish the provision’s applicability and the conduct before asking for conclusions about departure. An admission may support a proposition without resolving its causal significance or the full legal claim. Compare it with the other evidence.

Records-Preservation and Spoliation

Determine what evidence existed, who controlled it, when preservation duties arose, and what happened to it. A missing record can reflect several circumstances. Do not equate absence with negligent operation, intentional destruction, or entitlement to an adverse inference.

Analyze spoliation under the governing rule, including the required state of mind, prejudice, and available remedies. Document preservation requests and the chronology of loss. A preservation letter may give notice, but it does not automatically establish every condition for sanctions.

Model Preservation-Letter Contents

Identify the physical items, electronic data, and records requiring preservation and the people who control them. Request notice and an opportunity to document or inspect before changes where practicable. Address immediate rescue, safety, and environmental needs without demanding that a hazard remain active.

  • Relevant equipment in documented as-recovered condition, with a record of unavoidable emergency changes and preservation of removed components where feasible.
  • A sealed residual breathing-gas sample from any SCUBA tank before it is emptied or refilled.
  • All electronic data: dive-computer memory, vessel GPS and engine logs, and chemical-controller data, to be downloaded before overwriting or battery loss.
  • All surveillance and other video, secured before the retention period expires and it is overwritten.
  • All facility records: chemical and maintenance logs, inspection reports, service records, staffing schedules, certifications, and incident reports (this and prior incidents).
  • Documentation of the site and electrical configuration before avoidable alteration, while qualified personnel isolate immediate hazards.
  • All policies, procedures, manuals, and the operator’s adopted industry standards.

State the requested preservation steps and reserve appropriate remedies if evidence is lost. Counsel should assess duties independently of the letter and follow up on time-sensitive items. No letter guarantees preservation or the viability of a claim.

Chapter 18

Case Acceptance & Triage

Evaluate the evidence, unresolved questions, legal requirements, deadlines, likely costs, and potential recovery before accepting or declining a matter. An initial assessment should distinguish missing information from evidence that affirmatively undermines a claim.

Issues requiring further causation assessment
