  • A medical condition that may have contributed to incapacitation. Assess its actual role and whether environmental or operational factors also contributed.
  • The physical evidence has already been altered or destroyed: gear serviced, marina rewired, pool re-plumbed, vessel sold or repaired.
  • A reconstruction dependent on uncertain estimates. Determine whether records, testimony, testing, or bounded ranges can support those estimates.
  • Toxicology findings whose timing, interpretation, functional effects, and legal significance require qualified assessment.
  • An alleged standard violation with an unresolved causal relationship to the injury. Do not assume relevance or irrelevance from the violation’s label.
  • Conflicting or potentially interested witness accounts. Evaluate the basis, consistency, and corroboration of each rather than rejecting testimony by category.
  • The applicable law (e.g., DOHSA) sharply limits damages, making the economics unworkable even if liability is clear.

Evidence and practical considerations at intake

  • Evidence of compliance or departure from applicable requirements, together with its possible relationship to the incident.
  • Preserved physical evidence and hard data: an intact dive-computer log, surveillance video, measurable voltage in the water.
  • Evidence supporting legally recoverable economic and non-economic losses, without relying on presumed jury sympathy.
  • A documented pattern of prior incidents, warnings, or deferred maintenance supporting aggravated or punitive claims.
  • A well-capitalized, well-insured defendant reachable through a clean corporate-liability chain.
  • A reconstruction that addresses physical, medical, and human factors with supported assumptions and identified uncertainty.
  • A governing-law regime (favorable state wrongful-death statute) that permits broad non-economic and society-loss recovery.

Questions to Ask the Client at Intake

  1. Exactly where and when did this happen, what body of water, what facility, how far from shore?
  2. Who owned and operated the facility, vessel, or marina, and was there any warning or briefing?
  3. What is the victim’s relevant history, swimming ability, certifications, medical conditions, medications?
  4. What physical evidence still exists, and who has control of it right now?
  5. Is there any video, and how long before it is overwritten?
  6. Who witnessed the event, and are they available and neutral?
  7. Has anyone, the facility, an insurer, an investigator, already been in contact, and what was said or signed?
  8. What was the victim’s economic situation and family dependency?
  9. Has an autopsy been performed, and what did it find?
  10. Has any evidence already been altered, repaired, or discarded?

When to Pass, and Why

Before declining for weak causation, determine which elements lack support and what reasonable investigation could resolve them. A medical condition, altered item, or competing explanation does not automatically defeat a claim. Evaluate the applicable burden, possible concurrent causes, costs, deadlines, and remedies together.

An early expert consultation can identify technical questions and preservation needs. Ask what evidence is still required and what limits apply to the preliminary assessment. Do not treat a fixed consultation period or one calculation as a complete acceptance decision.

Expert-retention terms

Define consulting or testifying scope, compensation, access to evidence, and file-handling obligations in the engagement. Preserve the expert’s independence and ability to reach an adverse conclusion. Clear terms support the work but do not establish the reliability of a later opinion.

Document consulting and testifying responsibilities and any change in designation. Analyze the resulting discovery obligations under the applicable rules. Do not assume that an early consulting role protects all later use of the same work.

A Structured Intake Protocol

Use an intake checklist covering location, parties, deadlines, reported sequence, evidence custody, medical information, legal issues, expertise, cost, and collectability. Prioritize urgent preservation or filing needs rather than imposing a rigid sequence that delays them.

Record the reasons for the intake decision, the assumptions, and material information still missing. Reassess when new evidence or legal developments change those assumptions.

Ethical and Practical Considerations in Expert Retention

The engagement should define responsibilities without requiring a preferred conclusion. Check the applicable ethical, discovery, and disclosure rules separately. A well-drafted agreement does not guarantee compliance in practice, admissibility, or credibility.

Chapter 19

What to Expect from the Investigation

An investigation should document the evidence obtained, methods used, changes to the scene, and limits of the resulting analysis. Its scope and sequence depend on the incident, immediate hazards, access, and preservation needs.

Preservation priorities

Identify time-sensitive evidence promptly and assign responsibility for preservation. Relevant items may include:

  • All dive equipment, as recovered, unserviced and unwashed. Regulator testing comes later, under protocol, with a qualified technician.
  • A sealed gas sample from the cylinder, taken before the tank is emptied or refilled.
  • The dive computer and original available data, preserved and examined by a qualified person using a device-specific method.
  • Supervision records: buddy assignments, entry and exit logs, the roll call.
  • The rescue timeline: minutes from last seen to recovery, against the operator’s emergency plan.
  • Site conditions: visibility, current, temperature, weather.
  • The medical examiner’s full file, not the summary.
  • For a vessel: certificates, crew credentials, the casualty report, and the maintenance history.
  • For suspected electrical involvement: wiring configuration, connected equipment, protective devices, and records, documented while qualified personnel address immediate hazards.

Electronic equipment differs in what it records and how power changes affect stored data. Obtain qualified preservation instructions before avoidable operation, shutdown, or downloading. Document the device’s state and necessary emergency handling.

The Site Inspection

Arrange lawful site access through consent, applicable discovery procedures, or a court order. Define the permitted inspection and testing in a written protocol. Photograph and measure relevant conditions, including witness viewpoints, and identify changes since the incident. A later sightline observation is one part of the reconstruction, not a determination of the case.

Opening and Testing the Evidence

Establish notice, custody, and a documented protocol before testing or disassembly, subject to urgent preservation needs and applicable orders. An exemplar may help evaluate design or performance if its relevant differences are identified. Do not assume the incident item failed or that an exemplar reproduces its history.

Witnesses

Interview witnesses within applicable legal and ethical rules. Identify direct observations, timing estimates, prior statements, and potential sources of bias. A bystander, responder, or former employee is not automatically neutral.

Standards, scope, and applicable editions

Identify each potentially relevant statute, regulation, code, standard, and undertaking. Confirm scope, edition, adoption, and effective dates, including construction, alteration, and operating requirements. No single written standard necessarily defines every aspect of reasonable conduct.

Initial investigation checklist

  • Preservation letter out: gear, gas sample, dive computer, vessel records, electrical service.
  • Obtain device-specific instructions for preserving electronic data and document the as-found state.
  • Site access arranged: Rule 34 demand or written owner consent.
  • Identify witnesses and arrange legally permissible interviews.
  • Identify potentially applicable requirements and verify their scope, adoption, and dates.

Chapter A

Appendix

Key Federal and State Statutes

The Jones Act (46 U.S.C. § 30104)

Provides a negligence cause of action to seamen injured in the course of employment, with a ‘featherweight’ causation standard, the employer is liable if its negligence played any part, however slight, in the injury. Seaman status is determined by the Chandris substantial-connection test. The Jones Act claim runs alongside the general-maritime unseaworthiness claim and the seaman’s no-fault right to maintenance and cure.

Longshore and Harbor Workers’ Compensation Act (33 U.S.C. § 901 et seq.)

A federal workers’-compensation scheme for maritime workers who are not seamen, longshoremen, harbor workers, ship-repairers, and shipbuilders. Provides no-fault benefits and generally bars suit against the employer, but § 905(b) preserves a negligence action against a vessel whose fault caused the injury. Coverage turns on the status (maritime employment) and situs (covered maritime location) requirements.

Death on the High Seas Act (46 U.S.C. § 30301 et seq.)

DOHSA, 46 U.S.C. § 30301 et seq., may govern qualifying deaths on the high seas. Determine geographic coverage, claimant status, applicable exceptions, and available damages before applying its pecuniary-loss provisions.

Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (2007)

Review the Virginia Graeme Baker Act, 15 U.S.C. 8001 to 8008, and the applicable implementing regulation. Confirm the drain configuration, cover certification, service life, and any required additional protection. A compliance assessment and a causal opinion address different questions.

Model Aquatic Health Code (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

The national model code for the design, construction, operation, and management of public aquatic facilities. Current version: 5th Edition, posted December 2024, annex revised February 2025. It is not law anywhere until a jurisdiction adopts it, and jurisdictions adopt all, part, or none of it. It comes in two volumes: a code volume that states requirements and an annex volume that states rationale. Cite the code volume for duties and say when you are quoting the annex. Section numbering has shifted between editions, so confirm the pin cite for the edition in force on the date of loss.

International Swimming Pool and Spa Code (International Code Council)

The construction code for pools and spas in adopting jurisdictions. Lighting is Section 322 in the 2024 edition and Section 321 in the 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2021 editions. It contains no standalone water clarity section, handling water quality by reference to the pool and spa water quality standard.

American National Standards for pools and spas

ANSI/APSP/ICC-1 2014 (R2023), public swimming pools. ANSI/PHTA/ICC-2 2026, public pool and spa operations and maintenance. ANSI/PHTA/ICC-7 2020, suction entrapment avoidance. ANSI/APSP/ICC-8 2005, model barrier code, residential only. ANSI/PHTA/ICC-11 2026, water quality in public pools and hot tubs or spas. ANSI/APSP/ICC-16 2017, suction outlet fitting assemblies. The Association of Pool and Spa Professionals became the Pool and Hot Tub Alliance in 2019, so older standards keep the APSP designation and should be cited as issued.

National Electrical Code, NFPA 70, Articles 555, 553, and 680

Identify the NEC provisions applicable to the installation, including marina, floating-structure, and pool provisions where relevant. Grounding, bonding, and protective devices address different electrical hazards. Evaluate device function and the incident fault path separately; code compliance is not a guarantee against every possible injury.

NFPA 303, Fire Protection Standard for Marinas and Boatyards

NFPA 303 addresses marina and boatyard safety, including electrical systems, inspection, and maintenance. Determine the relevant edition, adoption, and provisions, then compare the evidence with those requirements. An alleged departure requires a separate causal analysis.

Statute Quick-Reference

  • Jones Act: 46 U.S.C. § 30104.
  • LHWCA: 33 U.S.C. § 901 et seq.
  • DOHSA: 46 U.S.C. § 30301 et seq.
  • Virginia Graeme Baker Act: 2007 (drain entrapment).
  • NEC / NFPA 70: Articles 555, 553, 680.
  • NFPA 303: marina fire/electrical safety.
  • Model Aquatic Health Code, 5th Edition (2024): clarity 5.7.6; lighting 4.6.1 and 5.6.1; glare 4.6.1.8, 5.6.1.2; surveillance zones 6.3.3.1.1; closure 6.6.3.1.
  • Drain covers: ANSI/APSP/ICC-16 2017 via 16 C.F.R. 1450.3.
  • Clarity by state: Florida 64E-9.004; Texas 25 TAC 265.193(e); New York 10 NYCRR 6-1.19(d)(2); California 22 CCR 65527.
  • Lighting by state: New York 10 NYCRR 6-1.29 item 7; Florida Building Code 454; California Building Code 3115B.
  • Always confirm the current text and the edition applicable to your facts.

Quick-Start Checklist for the New Aquatic File

Use the following checklist to identify urgent tasks and assign responsibility. Adapt it to the actual evidence, safety needs, and deadlines; no general list ensures that every preservation risk has been addressed.

  1. Send preservation letters the same day to every entity with possible control of the evidence, itemizing the physical items, data, and records to be preserved (see Chapter 17).
  2. Identify the case family (open water, pool/spa, SCUBA, ESD, boating, personal watercraft, maritime, cruise, resort) to determine the governing standards and defendants.
  3. For maritime matters, run the jurisdiction and choice-of-law analysis before choosing any theory; for cruise matters, read the ticket contract and calendar its deadlines immediately.
  4. Secure volatile data: download the dive computer, capture vessel logs, and lock down surveillance video before it is overwritten.
  5. Sequester the physical evidence unserviced; for SCUBA, capture a sealed residual-gas sample before the tank is touched.
  6. Obtain an early expert assessment of technical questions and missing evidence, without requiring a final causation opinion at intake (see Chapters 14 and 15).
  7. For suspected electrical involvement, coordinate documentation and evidence preservation with qualified electrical personnel and immediate hazard isolation.
  8. Map the corporate structure and insurance to assess collectability before investing in full workup.
  9. Analyze the damages regime (state vs. maritime vs. DOHSA) to confirm the case is economically viable.
  10. Make a documented accept-or-decline decision based on causation feasibility and collectability.

Standards Organizations

  • NAUI, National Association of Underwater Instructors: SCUBA training and operational standards; instructor certification.
  • PADI, Professional Association of Diving Instructors: recreational dive-training standards; determine the course, scope, and edition relevant to the activity.
  • SSI, Scuba Schools International: recreational dive-training standards.
  • RSTC, Recreational Scuba Training Council: cross-agency minimum training standards.
  • USLA, United States Lifesaving Association: open-water and beach lifeguard standards and agency certification. It does not write pool standards, and its guidelines publish no lifeguard-to-patron ratio.
  • Jeff Ellis & Associates (Ellis & Associates): the International Lifeguard Training Program, the 10/20 protection standard introduced in 1991, one-year lifeguard licensing, four hours of monthly in-service training, and unannounced facility audits.
  • American Red Cross: lifeguard training and rescue instruction; obtain the curriculum and edition actually used.
  • YMCA of the USA: aquatic programs and lifeguard training; identify the local program and curriculum.
  • PHTA, Pool and Hot Tub Alliance: pool and spa standards and operator education.
  • ICC, International Code Council: International Swimming Pool and Spa Code and other model codes.
  • NRPA, National Recreation and Park Association: aquatic-facility operator education.
  • IES, Illuminating Engineering Society: lighting recommended practices.
  • CPSC, Consumer Product Safety Commission: pool and spa product-safety regulation and submersion data.
  • ABYC, American Boat & Yacht Council: voluntary safety standards for boat design and onboard electrical systems.
  • CGA, Compressed Gas Association: Grade E breathing-air purity specification for SCUBA.
  • NFPA, National Fire Protection Association: publisher of the NEC (NFPA 70) and NFPA 303.
  • CDC Model Aquatic Health Code (MAHC): national model guidance for the design, operation, and management of public aquatic facilities. 5th Edition, 2024. Binding only where adopted.

Glossary of Aquatic and Maritime Terms for Litigators

Personal watercraft (PWC)
A vessel designed for an operator sitting, standing or kneeling on the craft rather than inside the hull, commonly using jet propulsion. USCG 2024 glossary.
Capsizing
Overturning of a vessel. USCG 2024 glossary.
Engine cut-off switch link
A device connecting the operator to an engine cut-off system, including physical lanyards and qualifying wireless arrangements. USCG, engine cut-off guidance.
Water-jet internal injury
Internal trauma from forceful water entry into a body cavity; distinguish this mechanism from blade contact. Yamaha, 2013 VXS/VXR manual.
Admiralty jurisdiction
For a tort, an inquiry into location and connection to maritime activity. Maritime-contract jurisdiction uses a different analysis; not every maritime claim requires the same location test.
Arterial gas embolism (AGE)
Gas in the arterial circulation. In a diving investigation, evaluate the proposed source and mechanism with the medical findings and dive sequence.
BCD (buoyancy compensator device)
An inflatable component used to adjust buoyancy. Its effect depends on gas volume, weighting, other equipment, and the diver’s actions.
Cold-shock response
Involuntary gasp and hyperventilation triggered by sudden immersion in cold water, capable of causing aspiration within seconds.
Decompression sickness (DCS)
Injury associated with inert-gas bubbles during or after decompression. Remaining within a computer or table limit does not eliminate the possibility. Divers Alert Network, Effective Use of Your Dive Computer.
Electric-shock drowning (ESD)
Drowning associated with electrical incapacitation. Evaluate exposure and medical evidence; absence of burns alone does not establish or exclude the mechanism.
Ground-fault protection (GFCI/GFPE)
Protective devices with different intended functions and trip characteristics. Identify the actual device and circuit; personnel and equipment protection are not interchangeable.
Hydrostatic pressure
Pressure exerted by water at rest, increasing about one atmosphere per 33 feet of seawater.
Instinctive drowning response
A description of observed behavior during difficulty maintaining the airway above water. It is not a universal sequence or an individual timing rule.
Laryngospasm
Involuntary closure of the larynx. Do not assume that it occurred or persisted for a particular interval without appropriate medical support.
Maintenance and cure
A seaman’s no-fault right to living expenses and medical care until maximum medical improvement.
Seaman status
The threshold requirement for a Jones Act claim; a substantial connection, in duration and nature, to a vessel in navigation (Chandris test).
Unseaworthiness
A vessel owner’s non-delegable, near-strict-liability duty to provide a vessel and crew reasonably fit for their intended use.
Virginia Graeme Baker Act
Federal pool and spa anti-entrapment law. Additional-system requirements depend on drain configuration; apply the statute and regulation to the actual installation.
Bather load
The number of people using the water. Distinguish this from an applicable theoretical peak occupancy calculation, which may include patrons outside the water.
Foot-candle
A unit of illuminance, one lumen per square foot. Pool lighting requirements are written in foot-candles at the water surface and deck, and in lumens or watts per square foot for underwater lighting.
Glare
Light that can interfere with visibility or recognition. Its effect depends on the source, surface, observer, and target conditions.
Imminent health hazard
A category used in the MAHC for conditions requiring correction or closure under its provisions. Verify local adoption and enforcement requirements.
Marker tile test
The model code’s clarity test: a contrasting tile, four inches square, or eight inches square in pools over ten feet deep, placed at the deepest point and visible from any deck point within thirty feet.
Nephelometric turbidity unit (NTU)
A measure of turbidity from light scattering. An instrument result and a visual test address different aspects of water clarity; use the applicable requirement.
RID factor
Recognition, intrusion, and distraction: a framework for examining surveillance problems, not an exhaustive explanation for every drowning.
Ten twenty standard
The Ellis and Associates protection standard: scan the assigned zone in ten seconds, reach the person within twenty. The model code adopts the twenty second reach and declines to set a recognition time.
Theoretical peak occupancy
The maximum number of bathers and patrons a venue may hold under the model code, calculated from water surface area and venue type.
Turbidity
Cloudiness associated with suspended material. Its effect on detection requires assessment with lighting, depth, viewing angle, and other conditions.
Utstein definition of drowning
The 2002 consensus definition: the process of experiencing respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid, with three outcomes, death, survival with morbidity, and survival without.
Zone of patron surveillance
The area assigned to a lifeguard. Verify the applicable requirements for coverage, visibility, and reach time rather than assuming one rule governs every facility.

About Steve Wolf, Full Biography

Steve Wolf’s work includes maritime, drowning, and SCUBA investigations. He is a NAUI-certified SCUBA instructor, a rescue diver, and an experienced Emergency Medical Technician. He holds a B.A. from Columbia University, has written eleven patents, and draws on experience as a private investigator.

Wolf has served as a maritime safety officer, rescue diver, and safety diver on movie sets and on the Shelby County Sheriff’s Office Dive Team. He holds seventeen FEMA certifications relevant to rescue, incident command, and hazard analysis. His media appearances include CNN, Fox News, MSNBC, and NewsNation.

His investigative work examines records, physical evidence, witness accounts, and relevant standards. Each assignment requires an opinion-specific assessment of qualifications, methods, supporting facts, and uncertainty.
